Sale of minor girls in Orissa 
DR. M. N. DAS (Orissa) : My Special Mention might be relating to a 
particular State of our country, but the evil mentioned therein might be 
prevailing in other parts of India. Sir, while poverty of the tribal people of 
Orissa, particularly in Kalahandi, Bolangir and Koraput region - infamous as 
the KBK - has reached abysmal depth, iron ically enough, taking advantage of 
the plight of the poorer people in coastal districts of Orissa, unscrupulous 
persons from outside are manipulating to smuggle out minor girls to other 
parts of India for making money from human misery. While a few instances of 
such deals come to light, majority of cases are never known. During 1994-
2001, according to Police sources, 3,286 minor-girls were reported missing 
from districts of Balasore, Bhadrak, ' Nayagarh, Cuttack and Mayurbhanj. 
While the Police could rescue only 516 of such unfortunate victims, the 
remaining hundreds remained untraced. Most of the victims belong to remote 
rural areas whose parents are too backward, besides being too poor, to try to 
recover their lost children. These children are perhaps sold for slavery purpose 
by inhuman locals to known agents from outside who are capable of deporting 
them to other States or even other countries.   It is also possible for merchants 
of death to steal human organs 
158 

[18 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
like eye or kidney for which organised rackets are working in our country. 
Nobody can ever know the fate of missing girl-children. While we talk of social-
justice, we talk of women empowerment and human rights, the stark reality at 
the lowest level speaks of a tragic tale. When parental affection proves 
ineffective before hunger and poverty, society has to intervene for effectively 
preventing abominable practices. Many measures can be thought of by the 
State Government and the Union Government, such as destitute homes for 
the unfortunates whose parents cannot feed them. I request the Centre to take 
up the issue seriously.

SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, last 
year, in the month of December, this House had a detailed discussion 
regarding disinvestment of both these oil companies. HPCL and BPCL. The 
Hon. Minister has given the reply to this House. But the Minister was not able 
to justify the reason for the disinvestment of the two companies, and still the 
cloud of doubt remains. Who is the real beneficiary from the disinvestment of 
these two companies? Whether the Government is able to convince the people 
of this country that by way of disinvesting these two oil companies, HPCL and 
BPCL, the Government or the people are going to be benefited by way of 
disinvestment. So, my first question to the Minister is: Who is the real 
beneficiary of this disinvestment process? It is being said that the proceeds of 
the disinvestment will be utilised in the social sector. As far as social 
commitment of this Government is concerned, suppose this Government is not 
convinced or not committed to the cause of the people, the cause of the 
working class, who are working in these public sector companies -- how can 
this Government fulfil the ambitions, or, fulfil the aims of the public at large in 
this country? So, the disinvestment is only to help the corporate houses. There 
is no doubt about that. We know what the corporate houses or the private 
companies are doing in this country. As far as NPA is concerned, it has 
crossed Rs. One lakh crores. Evasion of tax and so many other things are 
there. These two public sector companies are paying huge dividends. They are 
paying all legal dues to the Government. The exchequer is benefited by these 
two public sector companies. If these national assets are sold to the private 
corporate houses, from where will the wealth come in future? What is the 
apprehension of the Government and the Minister? They are giving an 
explanation that in future these companies will not be able to face competition 
and they will not be globally competitive. The statistics have come before the 
House. I am not going into the statistics because of lack of time. It is very well 
known that these two pioneer nava ratna companies are able to compete in 
the global scenario.    Then, why should they be

Collapse of Northern grid 
152. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that throughout the month of January this year, 
there was complete breakdown of the Northern grid and Delhi and 
neighbouring States went without power; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps taken to prevent the recurrence of such large scale power 
failure which takes place both in severe winter and summer with unfailing 
regularity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) No, Sir. There was neither 
any case of breakdown of the Northern Grid nor any incidence of Delhi and 
neighbouring States going without power during January, 2003. However, 
due to heavy fog and inclement weather during most part of January, 2003 the 
demand of power had substantially increased in Northern Region. On the other 
hand, the flow of power from the Eastern part of Northern Region to the 
Western part was restricted due to outage of one pole of HVDC Rihand-Dadri 
line and also on account of restrictions imposed on some trunk transmission lines 
due to foggy weather conditions.

[19 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Shortages in the Northern Region especially in peak winter and 
summer months occur due to wide gap between requirement and availability of 
power. To bridge the gap between demand and availability, the short and 
medium term measures taken are as under: 
(i) Enhancement of inter-state and inter-regional transfer of power. 
Arrangements have been made enabling transfer of 500 MW of 
surplus power from Eastern Region to Northern Region through 
the recently commissioned HVDC back to back station,  
(ii) Early stabilization of newly commissioned units and overall 
increase in plant load factor of thermal units,  
(iii) Reduction in transmission and Distribution losses, 
 (iv) Renovation and Modernisation of old and inefficient thermal 
generating units,  
(v) Strengthening/Augmentation of sab-transmission and distribution

(vi) Demand side management and promotion of energy efficiency 
and conservation measures, 
 (vii) Exploitation of hydro potential at a faster pace.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir, 
Hon'ble Prime Minister has launched a new initiative namely "Hariyali" on 
27.1.2003. Under this initiative, all watershed development programmes (DPAP, 
DDP and IWDP) of the Department of Land Resources would be implemented 
through Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRI).The basic features of "Hariyali" are 
given below: 
Under this initiative, the Gram Sabha would replace the Watershed 
Association and the Gram Panchayat would execute the watershed project with 
technical support from the Block Panchayat who would act as the Project 
Implementing Agency (PIA) for all watershed projects in a particular Block. In 
case the Block/Zilla Panchayat has no technical staff to support the Gram 
Panchayats, suitable Government Line Department/Autonomous Agency may be 
identified for the purpose. Failing all these options, a reputed voluntary 
organization (NGO) of good operational/Financial standing in the district with 
adequate technical expertise and experience would be identified to act as the 
PIA.This initiative is applicable to all new watershed development projects to be 
sanctioned in future.

Lower import tariffs on textiles products 
179. SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the India cotton textiles industry, especially the spinning 
segments, is seeking improved market access before it concedes to pressures 
for lower import tariffs on textiles products; 
(b) if so, whether industry representatives were involved in the high level 
meetings of the groups formed to suggest steps relating to market access 
negotiations with respect to textile items; 
(c) whether the Union Government has accepted the suggestions of the 
industry representatives which seeks greater market access; and 
(d) if so, the steps and assistance being provided to the textile 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANGOUDA R.  PATIL): (a) to (c) Tariff negotiations on non-
agricultural products, including textiles, has commenced in the World Trade 
Organisation (WTO) following the Doha Ministerial Declaration. The 
objective of the negotiations is improvement in market access, in particular on 
products of export interest to developing countries. Further, developing countries 
are expected to offer less than full reciprocity in reduction commitments. 
The Textile Commissioner had constituted two Industry Groups for 
making recommendations on market access negotiations for textile items. The 
Industry Groups which included, representatives from Cotton Textile Industry, 
had made recommendations to the effect that reduction of import duties for textile 
products in India should be proposed provided there was more than comparable 
reduction in the import duties of our major importing countries, our competing 
countries effected similar reductions and Government took necessary decisions 
for improving the competitiveness of Indian textile industry. 
122 

[19 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
At this stage the modalities for the negotiations are being discussed in the 
WTO and once the modalities are finalised the actual tariff negotiations would begin. 
India has submitted its proposals on modalities to the WTO on 30th December, 
2002 after holding inter-ministerial discussions and consultations with other 
stakeholders. 
(d) Government have been taking several steps from time to time to 
strengthen the textile industry. Some of the important initiatives are: 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(ii) Weaving, processing and garment machinery, which are covered under 
TUFS, have been extended the facility of accelerated depreciation at 
the rate of 50%. Cost of machinery has also been reduced through Fiscal 
Policy measures.This further encourages modernisation. 
(iii) Technology Mission of Cotton has been launched for initiating 
focussed steps for boosting production, productivity and quality of 
cotton for manufacture and export of competitive downstream textile 
products. 
(iv) With a view to encouraging backward integration, the custom duty 
on shuttleless looms has been brought from 15% to 5%. 
(v) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches and 
Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in the field of design, merchandising and 
marketing. 
(vi) Facilities by way of eco-testing laboratories have been created to enable 
exporters to get the textile products pre-tested for conforming to the 
requirements of importing countries. 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [19 February, 2003] 
(vii) For upgrading infractructure facilities at important textile centres, a 
scheme Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS) 
has been launched.

    Need for Adequate Allocation of Funds for Universalisation of Elementary 
Education 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, the Ninety-third 
Constitution Amendment Bill was passed by the Parliament last year to 
provide free and compulsory education to all children in the age group of 6-14 
years. The Tapas Majumdar Committee appointed by the Government had 
assessed the amount of financial requirements for this purpose at Rs. 13,700 
crores, according to the 1996 price index. The Ninety-Third Constitution 
Amendment Bill stated in its Financial Memorandum that the requirement 
would be Rs.9,800 crores. However, the Planning Commission provided for the 
current financial year a total amount of Rs.4,667 crores for the entire 
Department of Elementary Education. This amount is altogether inadequate. A 
single scheme of the Department, the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, needs Rs. 
7,350 crores annually. The Kothari Commission had recommended that, at 
least, 6 per cent of the GDP should be allocated for education. During the last 
decade, however, the State investment in education declined from an all-time 
high of almost 5 per cent of the GDP in 1991 to 3.6 per cent of the GDP in 
1997-98. 
I, therefore, urge upon the Government, firstly, to provide, at least, 
the amount mentioned in the Ninety-Third Constitution Amendment Bill for 
universalisation of elementary education in the next Budget; and, secondly, to 
ensure education of a reasonable quality for the children of socially and

Need for a Development Project for the Production of Compost Organic 
Manure From Non Milch Old Cattle 
SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA (Gujarat) : Sir, the cattle population of the 
country is estimated to be 29 crores. Considering the average availability of 
dung from an animal at 6 kgs. per day, we would get nearly 17.28 lakh MT of 
dung per day and 63.072 crores MT of dung per year. 
One kg. of dung produces 20 kg. of compost manure by adopting 
NADEP method. Even if we consider 7 kg. of compost organic manure from 
one kg. of dung, total production would be 449.49 crore MT of compost 
organic manure per year. At present, the cultivable land in the country is put at 
15 crore hectares. If 10 tonnes of compost organic manure is needed per 
hectare of land, the need would be only 150 crore MT of compost organic 
manure. This would eliminate the use of chemical fertilizers, insecticides and 
pesticides and save valuable foreign exchange. This would also preserve the 
fertility of the land and give better quality of agricultural products, fruits and 
vegetables. 
Old non-milch animal would produce 48 tonnes of compost organic 
manure which will fetch Rs. 48,000/- per year. The maintenance expenditure 
of an animal would not be more than Rs. 18,000/- per year. Thus, one animal 
can generate an income of Rs. 30,000/- per year. 
From a unit of 250 Non Milch cattle, 2000 kgs. of dung would be 
available per day, which would produce 85 million cu.ft. biogas. From this 
biogas, 130 kw/h (units) electricity can be produced at a generating cost of 90 
paise per kw only.

SHRI CO. POULOSE (Kerala): Sir, the co-operative sector in Kerala

sector is really a backbone to the agricultural development activities in Kerala. 
The main source of money of this sector for lending is the deposits received 
from various parties.

sector under Section 80(P). Immunity from deduction of tax on the interest 
received by the depositors under Section 194 of the Income Tax Act, is a policy 
for the orderly development of the co-operative sector in the country. Now, due 
to the notices issued by the Income Tax Department under Section 133(6) to 
furnish details of deposits made by the members, -the depositors are becoming 
reluctant to make deposits in the co-operative sector. This, in turn, is adversely

sector in the State. Also, due to this, lot of depositors are withdrawing their 
deposits from the co-operative sector.

in villages and major deposits are from poor villagers who had earned money 
by working very hard. The co-operative banks are providing attractive rate of 
interest compared to other banks.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, hon. Members have expressed their apprehensions about the 
repealing of this Act. I want to bring to your kind notice that this Commission 
was constituted in 1984. It has not been operational for the past 4-5 years. In 
the year 1985, Banking Service Recruitment Boards were established for 
recruitment of officers and clerks in the nationalised banks. After that the State 
Bank of India and its associate banks have been recruiting their officers 
through their Regional Recruitment Boards. It was again reviewed in 1987. 
After the review, it was found that the Banking Sen/ice Recruitment Boards 
were doing well. They are, certainly, doing their recruitment well. Hence, it is 
not necessary to have the Banking Service Commission Act, which is not 
being implemented. After that, the Financial Systems Committee, I mean, the 
Narasimhan Committee, recommended the recruitment policy and said that it 
was not necessary to keep it in the Statute Book. After that a Committee, 
under the Chairmanship of Dr. D.R. Mehta, Deputy Governor of Reserve Bank, 
recommended the repeal of the Banking Service Commission Act, 1984. After 
that, because of various reasons, we felt that it should be repealed. During 
2001-02, while presenting the Budget, the hon. Finance Minister said that 
since autonomy was given to the banks to recruit the personnel according to 
their needs, the RRBs and the BSRBs should be abolished and that the 
selection 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [19 February, 2003] 
process should be handed over to the respective banks. It was only after that it 
was abolished. So, this Service Commission Act is not necessary to be kept in 
the Statute Book. Hence, we have brought this repeal Bill. At the same time, 
some hon. Members wanted to know, if it is abolished, what is the alternative 
to the Reservation Policy. Hon. Members, Shri Shunmugasundaram, Shri 
Viduthalai Virumbi and Shri Lalu Prasad, have stated that it is an anti-Dalit and 
anti-poor Government. It is not like that. We are for the development and 
welfare of the poor people. We are adhering to our Reservation Policy and 
instructing the banks that, while recruiting officers of Class-I or Class-ll or 
Groups C & D employees, they should adhere to the Reservation Policy. The 
respective Bank Boards are given the power. They will adhere to the 
Reservation Policy in respect of SCs, STs and OBCs. They will do their 
recruitment, according to the Reservation Policy. If anybody fails in this 
respect, the Government will intervene and take necessary action and those 
who are responsible will be punished. I assure this House that the Reservation 
Policy would continue and it will be adhered to at all levels including Group-C 
arid Group-D. With these words, I request the whole House to approve this 
repeal Bill.

suffer a lot. Factors like their crop failure, economic losses and their inability to 
pay debt are forcing them to end their life. The trend shows suicide by farmers 
is rising. Every day, we read in newspapers about the farmer committing 
suicide for his inability to pay the loans he had taken for agriculture. In an 
agriculture predominant country, this should not happen. We have to find out 
both long-term and short-term solutions to the problem of drought in our 
country. 
Short-term solutions can include a better management of the existing 
water resources, crop planning rotation, proper guidance to farmers by the 
State Government and waiver of loans to farmers. The small and marginal 
farmers should be given due importance. They should be given financial 
assistance to withstand the drought conditions. They can be engaged in 
alternative jobs to help them economically. 
So far as long-term measures are concerned, linking of rivers, proper 
crop planning etc. are the solutions. The Government has initiated action on 
linking of rivers. This is a welcome step. Now, it is to be seen how the 
Government moves on this project. Let it not remain only on paper. 
The Government has also provided financial relief to the farmers in 
order to compensate them for the losses suffered in unirrigated areas in the 
form of a special Drought Relief Price ranging from Rs.5/- to Rs.20/- per 
quintal. This is inadequate. It should be raised to appropriately compensate 
the farmers. The States should also ensure a timely flow of institutional credit 
to the farmers. 
I am sorry to point out that the Central Government has not provided 
enough financial aid to the States. Against the demand for Rs. 1,562 crores 
made by the Karnataka Government, the Central Government has provided 
only Rs.221 crores. For Madhya Pradesh, against its demand for Rs.790 
crores, only Rs. 126 crores have been provided, and for Rajasthan, against its 
demand for Rs.7,519 crores, only Rs.207 crores have been provided. In total, 
as against the demand for Rs.31,102 cores, only Rs. 1,999 crores have been 
provided. 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [19 February, 2003] 
As per a study, the spectre of drought over a vast area of India could 
cost the Exchequer over Rs.1,000 crores. This means, allocation for 
development will be either reduced or diverted to the relief and rehabilitation 
schemes. 
There is a need to solve the inter-State water disputes amicably and 
in a harmonious manner so as to ensure an equitable availability of water 
during dry spells. In Karnataka, 186 taluks have been declared as drought-hit 
areas. The amount released to Karnataka is very meagre. Our hon. Chief 
Minister made repeated requests for extra foodgrains for "food for work" 
programme. But nothing has been done so far. I request the hon. Minister to 
release extra foodgrains to Karnataka as early as possible. It is also important 
to work out a viable water management system, in view of the unprecedented 
drought faced by the 14 States during the last year. Indian farmers are very 
hard working, but weather is not helping them. Drought and untimely rains 
frustrate their efforts. That makes them commit suicide. The worst sufferers are 
the small and marginal farmers and landless labourers. Government should 
ensure that these categories of farmers are not affected and they are properly 
compensated. Our hon. President, Madam Sonia Gandhi, has requested our 
hon. Prime Minister to make known in advance the entire allocation that could 
be given to each State, at least as a projection. So, our hon. Prime Minister 
should have taken that suggestion and made a note in advance to the States 
on the allocation they are giving to each State, and also released at least 50 
per cent of the capital initially so that the State can ensure an uninterrupted 
flow of foodgrains in the affected areas. Madam Sonia Gandhi also requested 
for delegation of powers to the Central Relief Commissioner to respond 
immediately to the distress signals from the State. Madam, unless you 
delegate the powers to Central Relief Commissioner, he cannot immediately 
respond, and he has to take long time because of the long process and the 
paper work, which takes long time. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY) in the Chair] 
So, it will affect the persons more and more.   I hope the hon. Minister will take 
these suggestions and help the people of our country.

(a) to (e) Government had strongly protested against the harassment of

Charge d'Affaires, are routinely subjected to threatening telephone calls, 
intimidatory and obstructive surveillance and offensive behaviour. 
Pakistan expelled four Indian officials on January 23,2003 and five 
more officials including the Charge d'Affaires on February 8, 2003.

approach of compulsive hostility, to the necessary measures Government had 
taken in view of the involvement of officials of Pakistan High Commission, 
including their Cd'A, in funding of terrorist and secessionist activities 
directed against India, and in activities incompatible with their official status.

bilateral "Code of Conduct for Treatment of Diplomatic/Consular Personnel 
in India and Pakistan" signed by the two countries in 1992, the responsibility 
for the safety and security of personnel of High Commission rests with the 
host Government. Government of India protests strongly to Government of 
Pakistan against all cases of harassment of officials of Indian High 
Commission in Islamabad and reminds them of their obligations under the 
Vienna Convention and bilateral Code of Conduct. Government remains 
committed to taking all necessary measures for the safety and security of the 
personnel in Indian Missions abroad.

Statement-1 
 IT. Schemes for rural areas 
1. The Department of Information Technology, Ministry of 
Communications & Information Technology has undertaken a scheme for 
setting up Community Information Centres (CICs) at 487 block 
headquarters in the seven North-East states and Sikkim for promoting 
application of Information Technology for accelerating socio-economic 
development of the region.The scheme is being implemented in the states 
of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, 
Tripura and Sikkim. 475 CICs have been setup till date. 
The project is mainly aimed at bridging the digital divide and providing 
connectivity at the grass root level particularly in those areas where the benefits 
of national development have not reached the community, specially women and 
children to the desired extent as they have all along been deprived of access to 
information relevant to their needs. 
2. E-lnfrastructure and E-Learning Group has no comprehensive 
scheme for rural and tribal areas. However, pilot implementation of Rural IT 
Centres (Samadhan Kendras) has been completed in Ramanathapuram Distt. of 
Tamil Nadu and 3 more Samadhan Kendra projects were launched in Ujjain (MP), 
West godavari Distt. (AP), and Chitrakoot (MP). Out of these Samadhan 
Kendra projects at Chitrakoot (MP) and Ujjain (MP), have been completed. 
These provide connectivity to internet as well as email and computer facilities 
to the villagers through localised centres. Besides this, a whole range of other 
information facilities required in rural areas are fulfilled through Samadhan 
Kendras. 
3. A Centrally Sponsored Scheme on computerisation of Land Records 
(CLR) is being implemented in the country since 1988-89 which included rural 
and tribal areas also. This Scheme is being implemented jointly by Minister of 
Rural Development and National Informatics Centre (NIC). Funds are being 
provided by Minister of Rural Development to States/UTs for installations of 
Computers at District and TehsilsAaluk centres and so far 582 districts and 
2959 tehsils/taluks/blocks of the country have been brought under the 
programme. 
4. Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission, under the Ministry of 
Rural Development provides assistance at the rate of 100 per cent to 
75 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
the States and Union Territories for procurement of hardware, office 
automation packages, training of manpower and development of application 
software for computerisation up to the division level officers of the line 
departments. 
5. The Ministry undertook a pilot project for providing VSAT 
connectivity to 15 District Rural Development Agencies (DRDAs) for 
providing internet facilities and a web based software for poverty alleviation and 
rural development programmes. The pilot project has been taken up in 15 
districts in 11 States, namely Anantpur and Nalgonda in Andhra Pradesh, 
Thanjavur and Perambalur in Tamil Nadu, Etawah in Uttar Pradesh, Hosangabad, 
Narisinghpur and Jaisen in Madhya Pradesh, Solan in Himachal Pradesh, 
Hazaribagh in Jharkhand, Midnapur in West Bengal, Shillong in Meghalaya, 
Chandrapur in Maharashtra, SJkar in Rajasthan and Almora in Uttaranchal. The 
project endeavors to establish a system for flow of information in respect of 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), Jawahar Grarri Samridhi Yojana 
(JGSY), Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), Indra Awaas Yojana (IAY) and 
Watershed programmes. 
6. Other projects being implemented by NIC jointly with concerned 
Ministers viz. Agricultural Produce Markets Networking of Mandis, Social 
Welfare Pension Computerisation. ICT applications in the Rural Development 
sector, includes: (a) CRISP: Computerised Rural Information Support Project — 
Rural Soft 2000: Processes of the data related to poverty alleviation schemes 
sponsored by MRD/SRD and implementation coordinated by DRDA. (b) Rural 
Bazar: An e-commerce solution that helps DRDA's in marketing of rural products 
of SGSY beneficiaries, (c) PriaSoft: Addresses the financial management needs and 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) such as Zilla Parishad, Block Samiti and Village 
Panchayat, and is being tested at SivaGanga, Tamil Nadu, (d) ENRICH: A 
generic solution by NIC and UNESCO for usage in Community Multimedia 
Centres (CMCs) that is a one stop access, communication & delivery 
mechanism for communities, customizable in terms of local, Indian language and 
content. 
7. In another noval scheme for developing IT application for the rural and 
poor people, Media Lab Asia has been set up by the Government as a research 
company with a network of national laboratories for research, innovation and 
development, of advanced ICT technologies for the benefit of masses. Media Lab 
Asia was launched in June 2001 jointly with 
76 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Massachusetts Institute of Technology  (MIT), USA. The objective of this 
scheme is to address trie grand challenges of poverty, literacy, education, health, 
employment, and micro-entrepreneurship through the use of information and 
communication technologies (ICT), on a large co-ordinated scale, using futuristic 
technology and both academic and non-academic input with creativity, 
sensitivity, and with a focus on affordable accessibility.

IT benefits to Hindi and other Indian languages speaking population 
Department of IT has setup 13 Resource centres for Technology 
Development in Indian Languages in various parts of the country. These centres 
have the responsibility of developing tools and technology for application/use 
of computers in all the 18 constitutionally recognised local languages of India. 
Localisation of technology and Content Creation in Hindi and making the 
content available on computer and Internet, is being spearheaded in Hindi 
speaking states under the programme: Content Development and IT 
Localisation Network (Coil-Net). 
Both the above initiatives of the Department of IT also directly/ 
indirectly benefit the rural masses. 
The IT projects implemented for rural areas by NIC (mentioned in 
Annexure I) are also in iQcal languages, and often use icon-based interfaces etc, in 
order to minimise difficulties experienced by literates/semi-literates. 
Samadhan Kendra projects already mentioned at 1.2 caters to the needs

Continuation of terrorism by Pakistan 
262. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to State: 
(a) whether there is no sign of Pakistan moving away from terrorism 
despite presence of Indian Army on the borders for a year; and 
(b) if so, the new approach proposed for a new foreign policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) President Musharraf committed on 
January 12, May 27 and June 6, 2002 that cross-border infiltration would be 
ended on a permanent basis, Pakistan would no longer allow its territory to be 
used for any terrorist activity anywhere in the world, and no organization in 
Pakistan would be allowed to indulge in terrorism in the name of Kashmir. 
However, cross-border infiltration aid terrorism still continue. 
Although, Pakistan took some initial action against some terrorist 
groups and arrested some low-level cadr es, there is no evidence of any firm 
action against the infrastructure in Pakistan that supports terrorism. There have 
also been reversals of some of the initial Pakistani steps including release of 
arrested terrorist leaders and cadres. Despite limited and reluctant support that 
the Pakistani establishment has provided to the international coalition against 
foreign Al-Qaeda elements, it has attempted to maintain its support and 
sponsorship of terrorist groups acting against its neighbouring countries. 
(b) The Government have been appropriately and effectively bringing to the 
attention of the international community facts pertaining to Pakistan's sponsorship 
of cross-border terrorism and are firmly resolved to take all necessary measures 
to fight against this menace. There is widespread recognition of Pakistan being 
the epicentre of international terrorism and several countries have called upon 
Pakistan to stop its sponsorship or continuing as 'platform* for international 
terrorism. 
India remains committed to resuming bilateral dialogue with Pakistan in the 
spirit of Simla Agreement and Lahore Declaration. But Pakistan must stop 
sponsorship of cross-border terrorism for dialogue to be held.

machineries to enforce child labour related provisions of the laws. 
Government of India has taken steps for withdrawal and rehabilitation of 
Child Labour working in hazardous occupations to reduce the incidence of child 
labour in a particular district through tfie Scheme of NCLR Under the Scheme, 
special schools have been set up in the child labour endemic districts with the provision 
for non-formal/formal education, vocational training, stipend, nutrition, health-care 
etc. So far, 100 NCLPs have been sanctioned in 13 child labour endemic districts 
for coverage of 2.11 lakh children. 
Government is committed to the goal of eradication of child labour in all 
its forms. Considering the nature and magnitude of the problem, a gradual and 
sequential approach has been adopted for withdrawal and rehabilitation of child 
labour, beginning with children working in hazardous occuptions.

Central Plan outlay for Ninth Plan 
293. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Central Plan outlay for the Ninth Plan has fallen short 
of the target by Rs. 82.786 crore; 
(b) if so, what was the actual realisation during the plan period; 
(c) to what extent it fell short of the projected outlay; 
(d) the reasons thereof; 
(e) what are the steps being taken to formulate the Tenth Plan in view of 
the experience gained during the Ninth Plan; and 
(f) what steps are being considered during the Tenth Plan to fully meet 
the targets? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (d) Against a projected outlay of 
Rs. 4,89,361 crore (at 1996-97 prices) for the Ninth Plan, the outlay 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
realized during the plan was Rs. 4,06,687 crore. The actual realization and the 
shortfall were thus 83.1 per cent and 16.9 per cent respectively of the outlay 
projected for the Ninth Plan. The main reason for the shortfall in the outlay during 
the Ninth Plan period was the substantial deterioration in the Balance from Current 
Revenues caused due to a stagnant level of tax revenues coupled with substantial 
growth in non-plan revenue expenditure. 
(e) and (f) The draft Tenth Plan document has been approved by the National 
Development Council. It outlines various measures for raising resources 
required for financing the outlay projected for the Tenth Plan. The steps aimed 
at increasing the tax revenues include-improving the coverage of service tax, 
reducing unnecessary exemptions, computerization of income-tax system, 
rationalization of customs and excise taxes and extension of Value Added Tax 
(VAT) at the state level and its integration with the Central VAT. The Tenth 
Plan document also suggests steps for controlling non-plan revenue 
expenditure and cost recovery through levy of user charges in order to 
improve the resource position of the Government.

DR. L.M. SINGHVI: Madam, it is a great privilege and a heart 
warning honour to move the Motion of Thanks to the President of India for 
his Address. The Joint Session of the two Houses of Parliament is a 
defmining annual parliamentary event, which marks the commencement of 
the First Session of each year, so very co lourfully. It is rooted in centuries of 
colourful evolution in the Westminster. But, the occasion is provided for in 
Article 87 of the Constitution of India, which enjoins on the President to 
address both Houses of Parliament, assembled together, and inform the 
Parliament of the causes of its summons. Article 87(2) provides that the 
Parliament shall discuss the matters referred to in the President's Address, and 
perhaps, taken strictly, it entitles us only to discuss what is referred to in the 
Address of the President. But, in practice, we appear to be quite oblivious of 
that limitation, as the various amendments to the Motion of Thanks, year after 
year, testify. Now, we do discuss the Motion of Thanks, and when we discuss 
it, what is mentioned in the Address, is discussed; all that is not mentioned in 
the Address, is discussed; and what should have been mentioned, is also 
discussed. We may discuss intentions, as well as omissions and commissions. 
What makes these discussions, therefore, is a seamless web, generality of the 
nature of our discussions, which provides a sprawling playground of issues 
and matters. 
The Joint Session of the two Houses of Parliament, Madam, is 
conventionally the only occasion when the President is in Parliament. The 
President's Address is a substantive document this year, and it is, I think, a 
happy balancesheet as well as a promising blueprint. Every paragraph of it is 
pregnant with ideas, with achievements, and with promises. It reflects an 
inclusive and an integrated approach, a vision and mission of India, and we 
ought to forge a broad-based national movement. Let us demonstrate that

times for the diaspora. But that word is no longer confined to the Jewish

which originate from one country and spread out to many others. The idea is

shaped the fortunes of those countries -- prior to the British colonial period

.of the country. One of my major criticisms is that the Presidential Address 
ignored the sad plight of the urban majority of the population in this country. 
They are affected by poverty and unemployment. They are living in the 
backward parts of the country and the unevenness in growth is growing. Of 
course, the debate is going on about the number of people living Below the 
Poverty Line, whether it is 260 million or not, I am not going into that 
question at present. But certainly, we will get an opportunity when we discuss 
about poverty, separately. The Presidential Address itself admits that the 
people living Below the Poverty Line will come to the tune of 26 crores. Why 
this is happening? After more than 50 years of Independence, why have we 
failed to tackle these important issues? Madam, not only this, unemployment 
is also growing. The Government is not giving us data regarding the number 
of people who are unemployed in this country. Many studies are there. It is 
estimated that the number of registered unemployed people is about 4 crores. 
And as per the sample survey, the number of unemployed people in the rural 
areas is 8 crores. So, about 12 crores of people are unemployed in this 
country. There are also a lot of debates going on, but I am not going into that 
particular aspect of the matter.   Why have we failed to solve 
276 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
this problem of unemployment? There is another issue, I agree that many a 
people living Below the Poverty Line are coming out of poverty, but it is also 
a fact that a section of the people who are living Above the Poverty Line are 
going down to the level of Below the Poverty Line. Why this is happening? 
Why have they failed to tackle this important issue? It is also a fact that 
certain parts of our country which are advanced, are becoming more advanced 
and which are backward are becoming more backward. Why this kind of 
unevenness is prevailing there? Why sectoral unevenness is growing? 
It is also a fact that because of poverty, unemployment and 
backwardness, a considerable portion of our population, living in different 
parts of the country, is migrating from one place to another. This also has a lot 
of economic and social consequences; very serious adverse consequences are 
there. Why are these things happening in our country? Of course, the 
President's Address speaks about the rate of growth of the GDP. It says that 
the Tenth Five Year Plan would be able to achieve 8% growth in GDP. I am 
not going into the question whether we will be able to achieve it or not. 
Certainly, we are going to discuss this matter, when we take up the Tenth Plan 
for discussion. The main issue that we should address is how we should tackle 
the issue of poverty, how we should tackle the issue of unemployment and 
backwardness in this country. If we do not address these issues, I feel it is 
meaningless whether we are able to achieve 8% or 7% or 6% or even 10%. 
The main aim should be to solve the problems of a considerable section of our 
population. There is no doubt that we have had achievements in various fields 
during the post-Independence period. But the wealth that we have created 
during this period has not solved these major issues. Why have we failed? I 
feel it is because of certain defects in our development strategy that we have 
pursued during the post- Independence period. Actually, the development 
policy that we have pursued, is no doubt a capitalist development policy 
based on the interests of the richer sections. It is because of that that we have 
not been able to solve the problems of poverty, unemployment and the 
problem of backwardness. So, we need a new development strategy and a 
strategy based on the interests of the overwhelming majority of the population 
of our country and the poorer sections of this country. Without that, these 
problems cannot be solved. We have been pursuing a policy since 1991 - the 
policy of reforms, the policy based on liberalisation, privatisation  and 
globalisation.     Actually,  these new sets of polices  are 
277 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
aggravating the problems that we are facing in our country. The poorer 
sections are adversely affected because of these policies. Sir, look at the 
agrarian situation. The Leader of the Opposition has already explained this 
situation here. The present set of policies are not helping in increasing the 
productivity and production in agriculture. If we compare the pre-reforms 
period with the post-reforms period, it shows that the rate of growth has 
declined during the post-reforms period. The Planning Commission has made 
a detailed study, in the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Ninth Five-Year Plan, 
about the growth trends during the pre -reforms period and the growth trends 
during the post-reforms period. I may be allowed to read a portion from that 
Report. "During the 90s - 1989-90 to 1 998-99 - the growth rate of production 
of both foodgrains and non-foodgrains, taken together, has declined to 2.35 
per cent per annum from 3.72 per cent per annum. During the 80s - 1979-80 
to 1989-90 - the decline in the rate of growth of foodgrains was sharper  - 
from 3.54 per cent to 1.8O per cent per annum". 
Even for the milk and egg sector, which had led the growth pattern 
in the eighties', there was a decline in the nineties', although not as severe as 
for foodgrains." When the new set of policies were introduced, were initiated, 
it was explained that the new set of policies is going to help to attract more 
investments in agriculture, that will increase productivity and production, but 
the reverse is happening. Sir, the reverse is happening, the rate of growth is 
declining. 
There is also a mention in the President's Address about the credit 
facilities. The Leader of the Opposition has already explained about that. It is 
a fact. Our experience is, there is a shrinkage of institutional credit facilities in 
the rural countryside. In accounts; yes, there is an increase, but in reality, the 
poorer sections, who constitute the overwhelming majority, are not getting the 
institutional credit facilities. Now a new set of moneylenders are coming into 
rural countryside; they are exploiting the poorer sections; they are fleecing the 
poorer sections. Many of the suicides are taking place in the rural countryside 
because of the exploitation of the moneylenders. Why is this happening? 
Despite the tall talk about increasing the amount -of credit facilities, it is not 
really happening. The Leader of the Opposition has already explained the 
very same, because the President's Address is giving an entirely different 
picture, from what was explained by the PJanning Commission in the Mid-
term Appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan. There also,   I  would  like to 
quote a particular paragraph about this particular 
278 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
aspect. "According to RBI Report on trends and progress in banking, 1998-
99, the relative share of agricultural credit in the net bank credit stood at 12.8 
per cent in March, 1997 and 11.7 per cent in March, 1998 as well as in 
March, 1999. As against the target of 40 per cent for priority sector lending 
by banks, the sub-target for agriculture has been fixed at 18 per cent. The 
declining share of agriculture in the net bank credit against 18 per cent target, 
under priority lending, is a matter of concern. More credit needs to flow to 
agriculture for providing timely and adequate credit under simplified 
procedures to farmers for increasing agricultural production and 
productivity." 
Sir, there is a mention about the Kisan Credit Cards, here in this 
President's Address. Yes, a small sectio n has been given that benefit. There 
also, you can see the voice of the rich section. The poorer sections are not 
getting the benefits. Only the rich sections are reaping the benefits. So, how to 
cater to the needs of the poorer sections, that is the most important issue. 
There is a mention here that the Government has taken a decision to 
increase investments in irrigation. Sir, it is because of the new set of policies, 
the Government is retreating from all economic affairs, the Government is not 
making more investments in irrigation, not making more investments in 
power, not making more investments in science and technology, not making 
more investments in infrastructure facilities. Because of this, the agricultural 
production is not picking up; because of this, the poorer sections are mostly 
affected by that. Now, there is a mention in the President's Address that the 
Government is thinking of increasing more public investments. When the 
Government introduced this new set of policies, we pointed out that it is the 
public investments, more and more public investments, that attracted the 
private investment also. If there is decline in public investments, definitely, 
there will be decline in private investments also. Now, the Government is 
thinking. But it should not be confined only to the irrigation and irrigation 
alone. It should be expanded to expanding power facilities, expanding more 
investment in science and technology. Of course, because of our laboratories, 
because of our scientists, the high yielding varieties of seeds helped us in 
increasing the wheat production, helped us in increasing paddy production, 
helped us in increasing cane production and helped us in increasing the 
production of many other crops.   If you look at the investment in science and 
technology, 
279 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
there is a decline.   This is also affecting.   So, it should not be confined to 
irrigation and irrigation alone.   It should be expanded to other areas also. 
Sir, there is no mention about agricultural workers in the whole 
Presidential Address. They are the most exploited section in our society. They 
are suffering. Their workdays are declining. Their real wages are declining. 
There are various reasons for that. Shift from foodgrains to cash crops is one 
important aspect. The present trend more capital intensive agriculture is 
another aspect. The introduction of machinery in agriculture is taking place in 
a bigger way. All these things and many other reasons are there for the 
declining trend of the workdays and the real wages of the workers. The 
Government is not coming forward to protect the interests of the workers. 
Earlier the Government declared that they would bring forward a new 
legislation, a comprehensive Central legislation to take care of their interests, 
fixing the minimum wages and providing them social security measures. The 
Government is not coming forward. So, the Government is not taking care of 
the downtrodden sections of our society. There is no approach to address 
these problems. That is the tragedy of the country in the present situation. If 
you look at the industrial sector, the industrial sector is also not picking up. 
The cottage industries are in crisis, the handicraft sector is in crisis and the 
small and medium industries are in crisis because of the import of 
commodities from outside and because of the penetration of more and more 
multinationals and more capital-intensive industries. These sectors are facing 
difficulties. The privatisation policies are creating problems throwing many 
thousands unemployed. There is a mention in the Presidential Address in 
paragraph 42 that the Government is discussing about the Second National 
Labour Commission on Labour. I would like to quote that particular 
paragraph from the Presidential Address, "The Second Labour Commission 
on Labour has given a comprehensive report covering wide range of labour 
issues. Its specific recommendations are being discussed with various 
stakeholders." This is not a fact, Sir. This matter was discussed at the Indian 
Labour Conference in September last year. Then the Government assured the 
entire labour, the trade union leaders that the Government would discuss the 
Second Labour Commission Report with the trade unions and after that 
discussion they would come before the Parliament for enacting certain 
legislation. They have not discussed this issue so far. An entirely different 
picture is being portrayed here. That is not the fact. TheVe is also a mention 
about the Provident Fund.    Under the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme 
which benefits 3.17 
280 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
crore subscribers, a novel programme to reduce claim settlement time from 
30 days to one or two days has been introduced. But what is the reality? Why 
do you portray an entirely different picture than the reality? What is really 
happening is that the interest rate on the Provident Fund has been reduced by 
the Government from 12 to 9.5 per cent. This is some sort of a retirement 
benefit for the workers. The Government has reduced it! What is the amount 
of loss sustained by the workers due to reduction of one per cent interest? 
The reduction is estimated to be to the tune of Rs. 2,500 crores. So, on the 
one hand, there is a decline in the amount of money that the workers are 
getting. There is a reduction of money to the tune of Rs. 6,000 crores because 
of the reduction in the rate of interest introduced by the Government. On the 
other, the Government is saying. 'Oh, we have reduced from three months to 
two days.' Explain to the country. The people cannot be confused. These 
gimmicks in such declarations cannot hoodwink the people. The reality is 
this. Not only that, the Government is thinking of introducing certain 
legislations curbing the trade union rights of the workers in this country. The 
Government is trying to introduce the hire-and-fire policy. The Government 
is trying to take away the right of the workers to organise themselves and also 
their right of a collective bargaining. The Government is also not activising the 
Tripartite Consultation System. There are thirty-five Tripartite Consultative 
Committees. The Government has not convened any meeting. Sir, only five 
or six or seven meetings were held during the last one year. So, the 
Government is determined to make a big attempt on the workers in this 
country. Of course, they will try to resist such attacks. All the trade unions in 
this country have taken a decision to organise a demonstration on 26 m of this 
month. 
There are certain references on the Foreign Policy position of the 
Government in this Address. Some aspects have been mentioned by the hon. 
Leader of the Opposition. But, many other paragraphs have dealt with certain 
other aspects. But, what is the overall assessment of the Government on the 
existing world situation? What is the long-term perspective of the 
Government? How is the Government trying to proceed further? What are the 
short-term measures that the Governme nt is going to take to tackle the 
emerging world situation? According to us, the emerging world situation is a 
very, very dangerous one. According to us, the major threat emerging is the 
threat of American imperialism. They have attained the military superiority.    
They have very sophisticated nuclear weapons at 
281 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
their disposal. They also have a very sophisticated delivery system and are 
trying to perfect it through their National Missile Defence System. They want 
to take these arms to the outer space. Sir, such attempts are taking place. And, 
they have the National Security Strategy Document. Of course, now, it is a 
public document. In the Document, they have said, "Yes. We have been able 
to attain the superiority in arms and we will not allow any country to catch up 
with that. If anybody tries to catch up with us, we try to pre-empt it by using 
force." Sir, American imperialism is trying to make use of their military 
superiority to establish their domination on the economic life of other 
countries and on the political life of other countries. That is the major threat 
emerging in this world. How is the Government going to react to this 
emerging threat in this world? 
There is a casual reference on Iraq in this document. The present Iraq 
situation is the reflection of American aggression. America first said, "We 
need a regime change there." What right has America got to change the 
regime there? The American President went to the United Nations and 
threatened it to fall in line with American aggression, and if it did not accept, 
the USA will go ahead. The United Nations passed a resolution and sent a 
Team of Inspectors to Iraq. But they did not find anything there. Now, 
America says, "Whatever be their findings, we will go ahead with our 
programme." It will have very, very serious repercussions on the economy, on 
the life of the country. We are facing ve ry serious difficulties. The oil prices 
will shoot up. Many Indians are working in the Gulf countries. They will have 
to flee away from there. But these are not the only adverse affects. If America 
succeeds in its attempt, the emerging world would be a very, very dangerous 
place to live in. Our sovereignty will be impaired; our hard-won 
independence will be impaired. They will be the dictators, and will dictate 
what policies other countries should follow. We are failing in the WTO 
negotiations. How America is trying to influence the WTO? How America is 
trying to influence other countries? They try to browbeat others. How is the 
Government going to react to this emerging dangerous situation? A new 
approach is required. We have to build bridges with other countries. The 
entire world is resisting the American aggression. Last week, about 600-700 
cities have risen against American imperialism. The demonstrations are taking 
place. Millions and millions are taking part in those demonstrations. Their 
own allies are coming to resist America. But our Government is keeping 
silent. The Government is not coming forward. I am not going into the other 
details with regard to the Iraq issue.    If we 
282 

[20 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
discuss it separately, we will be able to go into all these aspects in detail. So, 
the Government should explain to us as to what is its attitude. 
There is a very casual reference about the 'non-proliferation'. 
Pakistan is helping People's Democratic Republic of Korea. Many other 
countries have double standards. The question is, how can our interests be 
protected? Non-proliferation alone cannot protect our interests. When India 
made nuclear tests, America and many other countries exploded. We disagree 
with that. That is a wrong decision. That facilitated our isolation among Non-
Aligned countries. Of course, that is entirely a different matter. I am not 
going into those details. But how can our interests be protected in the present 
world? We will have to take the issue of disarmament issue. We have to 
stage; we have to rally other countries behind us. Disarmament of major 
nuclear powers will help us to protect our national interests, our independence, 
our polices because in the emerging world, we cannot pursue our policies. 
America is going to dictate. So, we should take up these issues and should try 
to rally other countries for disarmament of major nuclear powers. 
The Leader of the Opposition has already explained the attitude of 
the Government with regard to protecting the secular polity of our country. 
How are they going to deal with this Ayodhya issue? The Government has 
now taken a more partisan attitude, and the Government is surrendering to 
communal fanatism more than in the past. I have with me the speech made by 
the President on 25 ,n February, 2002. I quote, " The Government of India, 
being the statutory receiver, is duty bound to maintain the status quo at the 
disputed site in Ayodhya. It will also ensure that all necessary measures will 
be taken to ensure the preservation of law and order." This statement has to 
be viewed in the background of the Supreme Court's decision taken in 1994. I 
am reading a relevant portion from the Supreme Court judgement reported in 
(1994) 6 SCC page 360, Para 49. I quote, "...The justification given for 
acquisition of the larger area including the property respecting which title is 
not disputed, is that the same is necessary to ensure that the final outcome of 
adjudication should not be rendered meaningless by the existence of 
properties belonging to Hindus in the vicinity of the disputed structure, in 
case the Muslims are found entitled to the disputed site. This obviously 
means that in the event of the Muslims succeeding in the adjudication of the 
dispute requiring the structure to be handed  over  to  the  Muslim  
community,   their  success  should   not   be 
283 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
thwarted by denial of proper access to, and enjoyment of rights in the 
disputed area by exercise of rights of ownership of Hindu owners of the 
adjacent properties...." So, the Presidentia l Address of the last year should be 
viewed in this background of the Supreme Court's decision. What is the 
present position of the Government? The Government has approached the 
Supreme Court. The Government has now changed its position from its 
earlier stand and became a party; it has become a co-petitioner of the VHP 
and other Hindu fanatics.   It is a very dangerous thing. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI NILOTPAL BASU) In the Chair] 
Sir, not only this, there is also another reference in the present 
Presidential Address about the Government's stand on Ayodhya. I consider 
that to be an inappropriate reference, by the Government, in the Presidential 
Address. I may be allowed to read that particular portion from the 
Presidential Address, para 15, last sentence. I quote: " "While the judiciary 
should expedite its work and give an early verdict... " Sir, what does it mean? 
The Government is criticising the decision of the court saying that the court is 
delaying the matter and that it should expedite it. According to me, this is 
inappropriate on the part of the Government to put this thing in the 
Presidential Address. This is a sort of interference in the judicial process of 
the country ! Sir, why has the Government become a party to it?  Let the 
parties contest their case. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, the secular polity of our country is under 
great threat. I am not going into how they are going to change the textbooks, 
how they are going to change the history. A deliberate infiltration by certain 
communal groups is taking place in almost all academic institutions of this 
country. Agressive communal propaganda is being allowed in this country. 
So, the secular polity of our country is under severe threat. A deliberate attack 
is being made on the federal policy of our country. If we look at the 
references of the Twelfth Finance Commission, we will find that the 
Government is trying to force the States to fall in line with the policies of the 
Central Government. The Constitutional powers, the Finance Commission 
and the Planning Commission have become an instrument of pressurising the 
State Governments to fall in line. An attempt has also been made to bypass 
the Parliament. Yesterday, when we discussed the Disinvestment Policy of 
the Government, an attempt was made to bypass our Parliamentary 
institution.    They don't care about the 
284 

[20 February. 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
recommendations made by the Parliamentary Committees. They don't even 
consider those things. Yes, we may have differences with the Election 
Commission. We are bound to have differences. But, how should such 
differences be articulated? Such differences should not be articulated by 
maligning persons, by pointing out their particular religion. But, that way, 
attacks are being organised. 
If anybody tries to resist, if anybody refuses to fall in line, this sort 
of malicious propaganda is unleashed, fascist kind of attacks are organised. 
So, our Parliamentary system is under threat. The Constitutional institutions 
are under threat. There is also a mention about the internal security of the 
country. No doubt, cross-border terrorism is a major threat. Other threats also 
exist in our country. Arms mafias are th ere, drug trafficking is taking place, 
forest mafias are there, coal mafias are there, kidnappings are taking place, 
extortions are taking place. Their number is increasing day-by-day. Crimes 
against women and children are increasing. Many other terrorist groups are 
trying to establish their influence in different parts of our country. They are 
making use of the archaic land laws existing in certain parts of the country. 
They are making use of caste oppression. We should address all these 
problems, only then, the internal security will be strengthened. There are also 
complaints about police atrocities. How is POTA being used? When POTA 
was passed by Parliament, we from the Opposition opposed it. Because we 
were afraid that it could be used against the political opponents. There is 
every possibility for that. The present experience in UP, the present 
experience in Tamil Nadu, the present experience in Delhi, are all examples 
of POTA being used against political opponents. This danger is there. How 
can we save the democratic rights of the people? It can be possible if POTA is 
scrapped. There is no need for POTA. Sir, the Government is trying to cover 
up its weaknesses and shortcomings. Our people are very cautious. They are 
not confused. The Government cannot hush up these matters. As you are 
observing, many spontaneous struggles are taking place, many organised 
struggles are taking place. The people are coming forward to resist the anti-
people and anti-national policies. 
Sir, only by strengthening and forcing the Government to change 
these policies can we save the country, and also the interests of the people of 
this country.   Two types of broad movements are required in this country. 
285 

RAJYA    SABHA [20 February, 2003] 
4.oop.m. 
One, a broad secular unity is required to protect the secular polity of our 
country, and, two, to take care of the interests of the poorer sections, in order 
to introduce a new set of development policy, a broad United Front is 
required in this country. 
So, I would request the Government, I would request the Mover of 
the Motion of Thanks to respond to the points raised by me. 
With these words, Sir, I conclude.

and learned speech from a senior Member of the House, Dr. Singhvi, moving 
the Motion of Thanks to the President's Address. The President's Address, in a 
Parliamentary system of democracy, is not a report card in the sense that the 
President is reporting to the Parliament about the performance of the 
Government. It is a self-assessment report where the Government, on its own, 
makes an assessment of its performance in the last one year, indicates the line 
on which further action is to be taken on policy issues and on programmes. It 
is not expected to be a comprehensive report because within the timeframe, 
that is available, nobody can present a comprehensive report, covering all 
aspects of Government's policies and programmes. It is intended only to 
highlight a few areas which should be of interest to the Members of 
Parliament, and, therefore, to the people as a whole. I thought, in the Address, 
the President had dealt mainly with the working of the economy and the 
foreign policy of the country, and had not adequately dealt with a very 
important segment of our ambitions, aspirations, dreams, and, I would refer to 
the social sector. There is every reason to be proud of the achievements in the 
economy taking into account what happens in the world, as a whole, in the last 
one year, the slow-down of the economy all over the world, the great drought

production. In this background, the achievements of the Government, of 
course, deserves praise and approbation; and that is what the President had 
done. But, I am of the view that adequate importance should have been given, 
if not equal, at least adequate importance should have been given to the social 
sector, particularly, to education and health care. Mr. Vce-Chairman, Sir, if I 
am asked to make an appraisal of our achievements during the 52 or 53 years 
of our Republic and present in a very short form where we went wrong most, I 
will put my finger on the

policy, they say, "we are bound by our charter". When we find out the charter, 
it permits you to maintain quality education, and quality education cannot be 
introduced or maintained without financial support, then, they throw up their 
hands in helplessness. 
I have myself written to the hon. Minister saying that the whole 
system has to be changed otherwise we will have to write off education in this 
country. We will produce third-rate graduates from second-rate colleges, who 
will find themselves unemployed because they are also unemployable. There 
are a few institutions here and there which are able to manage and they are 
surviving as quality institutions. The point that I am trying to make is, if 
education is not given the importance that it deserves, we would be failing in 
the objective which we have placed before us of lifting India to the level of a 
developed nation in 2020 and that dream may have to be extended further by 
20 years more. 
Equally sad is the state of health care in the country. Under the 
Human Development Index criteria we are placed at 134: Many of the Sub-
Saharan countries of Africa, are much above us in the HDI. We are a country 
which produces satellites which go into the stratosphere. We have constituted 
an Atomic Energy Commission which with the help of other scientists has 
produced atom bombs. We can do anything that other scientists and 
technologists are boasting of doing. But, when it comes to health care, our 
standards are lower than some of the Sub-Saharan countries of Africa. That is 
why I say that we cannot meet the aspirations or fulfil the expectations of the 
people unless we give them proper health care and proper educational 
facilities.

My last point is, no mention has been made in this Address about 
good governance as an objective. This is a problem which is now looming 
large like a small speck. I am saying with full sense of responsibility that in 
many States there is no governance, leave alone good governance. Many 
States, because of various reasons, are plunged into anarchy. Mafia gangs 
have taken over and gang wars and caste wars are going on and the 
administration is just sitting back. In fact, in certain States, particularly in the 
North-East, I am told that the officers are paying tax to the people to make 
sure that their houses are not attacked. Good governance even in well 
administered States, will not qualify for good governance in the correct sense 
of the term. Good governance means, governance of Governments rooted in 
values, rooted in ethics and rooted in principles. If the Government does not 
show an example of being above corruption, or being in control of those who 
are indulging in corruption, how can we talk of good governance? Corruption 
in Government continues unabated in a worst form than ever before. We have 
developed a sort of tolerance to corruption. We have accepted it as inevitable 
in a system like this. Unless the Government shows its determination to fight 
corruption in its own house, we will not be able to tell doctors, educationists, 
businessmen, politicians, etc. that you should not be indulging in  corruption. 
Therefore, I consider this omission about the social sector and about good 
governance and the determination to fight corruption as a significant 
omission. I am not saying that I am not joining the Vote of Thanks. With 
these words of reservation, I join my voice with the Vote of Thanks that is 
proposed for the President for his Address. Thank you.

To prevent derailments and reduce their impact, some of the measures are as 
under: 
(i) A non-lapsable Special Railway Safety Fund of Rs. 17,000/-crore 
has been set up for renewal of over-aged assets and for safety 
enhancement works. 
(ii) All the production units, majority of repair workshops and large number 
of Sheds/Depots have achieved ISO 9002 certification for their quality 
maintenance system. 
(iii) Procurement of new generation diesel locomotives with enhanced safety 
features such as multi-re-setting vigilance control device, 
6 

[21 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
computer controlled brake system, extended dynamic brake and 
creep control to avoid wheel slipping. 
(iv) Fitment of micro processor control speed recorders to monitor speed 
of the train. 
(v) Procurement of simulators as training aid to improve training of 
running staff. 
(vi) Odour-cum-fume type hot box detectors are under lab tests for timely 
detecting and detaching hot boxes thereby preventing breakage of 
axle/journals on the run. 
(vii) New wagons being inducted into the system are equipped with more 
reliable Casnub Bogies and Air Brake System Bogie Mounted 
Brake System on wagons has also been developed. The use of 
Composition Brake Blocks on wagons is being progressively 
increased. 
(viii) Improvement in rolling stock design to reduce the impact of 
accidents and resultant casualties. 
(ix) There has been progressive increase in use of Tie Tamping and 
Ballast Cleaning Machines for track maintenance. Track Renewal 
Trains are also being used. 
(x) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of the 
track, sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and 
portable accelerometers are being used progressively. 
(xi) For detection of rail fractures/weld failures, adequate double rail 
Ultra Sonic Flaw Detectors have been procured. Self Propelled 
Ultrasonic Rail Testing Cars are being procured. 
(xii) Regular inspection of track at various levels is undertaken. 
(xiii) Training to Railway staff is provided immediately after their 
recruitment and thereafter their knowledge is refreshed periodically. 
Seminars, workshops and field demonstrations are also organized 
for 'permanent way' staff from time to time to enhance and update 
their knowledge. 
(xiv) Patrolling of railway track by gangmen is carried at vulnerable 
locations during monsoon, summer and winter. 
7 

RAJYA  SABHA [21 February, 2003] 
(xv) The specifications of rail steel have been upgraded and are in 
conformity with the International Union of Railways (UIC) 
specifications. 
(xvi) The track structure is upgraded on planned basis. 
(xvii) To keep the track in good condition, track renewals are carried out 
whenever it becomes due subject to availability of funds. 
(xviii) Derailment prone four wheeler wagons (CRT wagons) are being phased 
out of service. 
(xix) Closer liaison is being maintained with State Police Departments, 
wherever required for prevention of crime on Railway tracks and 
bridges. 
(xx) Instructions have been issued to reduce the number of fish plated joints 
wherever feasible and for burring of two fish bolts, one on each rail, at 
joints located in the stretches considered vulnerable. 
(xxi) An anti-theft elastic rail clip and fish bolt fastening is under 
development. 
(xxii) Stringent penalty to the extent of dismissal/removal from service is 
being imposed on officials causing serious accidents. 
(c) and ($) Yes, Sir. In the derailment of 7685 Kacheguda—Bangalore 
Express, 19 persons lost their lives and 78 persons were injured. The loss of 
Railway property has been estimated to the tune of Rs. 2.21 crores. 
Commissioner of Railway Safety/South Central Circle has submitted his 
Preliminary Inquiry report and has concluded in his provisional findings that 
"derailment of 7685 Kacheguda — Bangalore Express occurred due to 
tampering with the track by way of cutting of left hand side rail by hacksaw and 
thereafter pushing its Pagidirai end inside by an unauthorized persons other than 
Railway staff". The accident falls under the category of "Tampering with track by 
persons other than railway staff".

*62.  SHRIMOTILALVORA: 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:† 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have worked on strategic plans to counter the 
drought in the coming year, in dry State like Rajasthan, Gujarat, M.R etc.: 
(b) if so, the highlights of such a plan; 
(c) if not, whether Government realize the planning to counter drought 
conditions needs to be done in advance; and 
(d) if so, what steps Government propose to take to protect the 
standing crops when the drought conditions arise this summer? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Measures to protect crops from drought this year or to deal with 
the situation if a drought recurs in the 'coming year 1 require short term 
measures through Contingency Plans to be drawn up and implemented by the 
State Governments concerned, with Central Government extending assistance 
whenever required. 
For States like Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat considerable 
area has remained unsown even in Rabi due to the lingering effects of 
drought. For area which were sown, however, the State Governments have 
made adequate arrangements to provide irrigation and other inputs including 
supply of electricity for operation of pumps and tube-wells. No serious damage 
to such crops, is, therefore, apprehended during the "summer months", unless 
there are large scale diversions of water for irrigation, for drinking water 
purposes.

(ICAR) exist), cultivation of fodder crops, measures for employment 
generation and emergency supply of water etc. In the event of damage to

(a) to (d) The University Grants Commission (UGC) releases grants 
only to those universities and colleges which are recognized in terms of

The UGC had identified 18 Fake Universities/Institutions functioning

five institutions have since been closed down. The Government of India/UGC 
has not provided any grant/aid to any fake university or college. 
 
As soon as the UGC gets to know about the existence of a fake 
university/institution, the promoters are advised immediately to stop their 
activities. Simultaneously, the State Government in which the Institution is 
located, is apprised of the matter with the request to take necessary action 
against the Institution as per the law. 
About fraudulent schools, no State Government has provided such 
information to the Central Government.

(a) The Government has taken the following steps under different

National Environment Awareness Campaign (NEAC) involving 
about 5000 to 6000 Non-Government Organisations (NGOs) is

been sponsored.

been initiated by taking up a pilot project in eight States namely 
Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Goa, J&K, Maharashtra, Orissa, Punjab
