Increase in AIDS cases 
545. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite the country spending around $40 million 
on its AIDS Control Programme, the incidence of this disease are still on the 
increase and is likely to grow from 4 million cases to 8.9 million by the 
middle of this decade; and 
(b) if so, the steps Government have taken to prevent the spread of this 
disease in the country and to bring awareness among the people to check the 
disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) In order to track the 
trends in the spread of HIV infections in the country, the National AIDS 
Control Organisation conducts a nation-wide sentinel surveillance round each 
year. This data is also used towards estimation of total HIV infections in the 
country, taking into consideration certain assumptions finalized after 
consultation with the national and international experts. The National AIDS 
Control Organisation has not made any future projection in respect of the 
number of HIV infections. 
Accordingly, the numbers of persons infected with HIV were 3.5 million in 
1998; 3.7 million in 1999; 3.86 million in 2000 and 3.97 million in 2001. These 
estimates indicate that there has not been any unsurge in the spread of HIV 
infection in the country. However, this number is a cause of concern and there 
can be no slackening of efforts to prevent and control the spread of this 
disease. 
In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, Govt, of 
India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control Programme, currently 
under implementation throughout the country as a centrally sponsored 
scheme with the following components:— 
Preventive interventions for high risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer counseling and 
behaviour change communications. 
Preventive interventions for the general population through programmes 
for blood safety, voluntary counseling and testing services, 
153 

RAJYA  SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
information education and communication(IEC) and awareness building among 
adolescents and sensitization for the AIDS Vaccine Initative. 
Provision of low cost care and support services by providing community 
care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and prevention of 
occupational exposure. 
Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including interventions and public-private partnerships. 
Build technical and managerial capacities for programme implementation 
through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and Evaluation, Technical resource 
groups, operational research and Programme Management. 
In order to increase awareness among the general population in order to 
motivate behaviour change, the State AIDS Control Societies are 
implementing various IEC activities under the programme. National AIDS 
Control Organisation is utilizing the services of the different units of the 
Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and Prasar Bharati 
(DOORDARSHAN & AAKASHVANI) for dissemination of messages. 
Services of Directorate of Advertising and Visual Publicity. Song and Drama 
Division and Press Information Bureau are being used for outreach activities using 
print, electronic and outdoor media, in various parts of the country. 
For sensitization of children and young people, School AIDS Education 
Programme, the UniversitiesTalk AIDS and VillageTalk AIDS Programmes are 
being implemented in collaboration with Ministry ofYouth Affairs and Sports. 
The programme has an inbuilt monitoring and evaluation component, which 
tracks the implementation of various components of the programme and also 
ensures evidence based programming.

Eradication of leprosy 
556. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have set any target for the eradication of 
leprosy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the measures adopted to achieve the above objectives? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) In conformity with the 
WHO global strategy, the Government of Indian has set a target for 
elimination of leprosy which means bringing down the prevalence rate of 
leprosy to less than one case per 10,000 population at the National level by the 
end of the year 2004-05. 
165 

RAJYA  SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
(c) National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) is a 100% 
Centrally sponsored scheme with the objective of achieving elimination of 
leprosy i.e. Prevalence of less than 1 case per 10,000 population at National 
Level by the end of the year 2004-05. 
The measures adopted under the Programme are: 
(i) Decentralization & Institutional Development under which State 
Leprosy Societies have been formed in 27 major States and District 
Leprosy Societies in all the districts in the country. 
(ii) Integration of leprosy services with General Health Care system in the 
country. 
(Hi) Two rounds of Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaigns for case 
detection throughout the country during 2001 -02 and 2002-03. 
(iv) Early Leprosy Case Detection and Free Multi Dr^gTherapy to all 
patients through all Government Primary Health Centres, 
dispensaries and Hospitals in the country. 
(v) Special Action Projects for Elimination of Leprosy (SAPEL) and 
Leprosy Elimination Campaign (LEC) for difficult/inaccessible/ 
under served Rural & Urban areas, respectively. 
(vi) Intensified Public Awareness Campaigns. 
(vii) Training of health staff in disability prevention and care. 
(viii) Training of General Health Care Staff in Leprosy.

Complaints against Judges of High Courts and Supreme Court 
588. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of complaints of misbehaviour, misconduct etc. received 
against the Judges of High Courts/Supreme Court during the last two years; 
(b) the action Government have taken against them; 
(c) whether there is any proposal under Government's consideration to 
empower the Chief Justice of India to ta ke punitive measures against erring 
Judges; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and by when it is likely to be brought 
forward? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): 
(a) to (d) The issue of Judicial Accountability was discussed at the 
Conference of Chief Justices held in 1990 and on the basis of the broad 
consensus emerging out of the deliberations, the Chief Justice of India 
summed up the position as follows: 
"The Chief Justice of the High Court has the competence to 
receive complaints against the conduct of the Judges of his court and 
when he receives any he would look into it for finding out if it 
deserves to be closely looked into. Where he is satisfied that the matter 
requires to be examined, he shall have facts ascertained in such 
manner as he considers appropriate keeping the nature of allegations in 
view and if he is of the opinion that the matter is such that it should 
be reported to the Chief Justice of India, he shall do so. 
The Chief Justice of India shall act in a similar manner in regard 
to complaints relating to conduct of Judges of the Supreme Court and in 
regard to conduct of Chief Justices of the High Courts. On the basis 
of the facts ascertained, the Chief Justice of the High Court or the 
Supreme Court, as the case may be shall take such appropriate action 
as may be considered proper, keeping the interests of the judiciary as 
the paramount consideration."

Commission, which inter-alia would draw up a Code of Ethics for Judges of the

empowered to examine complaints of deviant behaviour of all kinds and

subsidy subject to a ceiling of Rs. 10,000/- per project, 15% of project cost as

Government and State Governments in the ratio 49:51 and the balance amount 
is provided as loan at concessional rate of interest by the National Safai 
Karamacharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC). In order to 
accelerate and energise the pace of NSLRS, the concept of Sanitary Mart has 
been introduced in the year 1999-2000 for rehabilitation of scavengers in groups.

Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993" has

MOTION OF THANKS ON PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS -- Contd. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Discussion on the Motion of Thanks on 
the President's Address.   Shri J. Chitharanjan. 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Madam Deputy Chairperson, I 
am grateful to you for allowing me to participate in this discussion. 
First of all, I would like to pay my homage to Late Kalpana Chawla 
and six other astronauts, who died in the recent accident in the disintegration 
of space shuttle, Columbia. 
Madam, then, I deal with the Iraq situation, in the President's 
Address. All of us know that, at present, the Iraq issue is of utmost concern for 
the entire international community and of course, for the Indian people also. 
Unfortunately, the Government of India has not made its policy clear in this 
respect. Paragraph 71 of the President's Address says, "We share the concern 
of the entire world on the unhappy situation relating to Iraq. We have deep 
interest in peace, stability and security in that region. We hope that the wisdom 
of the international community, expressed through the UN Security Council, will 
result in a peaceful resolution of this matter..." Yesterday, the hon. Prime 
Minister has made a speech at the business forum of the NAM. There also he 
did not spell out as to what exactly is the policy of India in this respect is. The 
sole Super Power, the United States, declares some of the States as rogue 
States or evil States. They say that 'the countries, which have large amount of 
arms, would be attacked1. They say that they would dictate terms to the United 
Nations Organisation itself. 
238 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
The Security Council is being asked to take a decision in their favour. And 
then they go on to say that even if the Security Council does not agree to their 
demand, they, along with their allies, would attack Iraq, and in that case U.N.'s 
existence will be in danger. This is what the American President, Mr. George 
Bush, is saying. Madam, if this thing is allowed to happen, what will be the 
outcome? America may attack Iraq tomorrow and the next day, Iran may be 
attacked and then, they may attack North Korea also, and then, some other 
country might be attacked. It might become the rule of the day; an unwritten 
rule of the day. The question is: Will we be spared? On the same ground, one 
day, India can also be attacked. In para 70, the President has stated this and I 
quote: "The Gulf region is of great importance to India. The region is a major 
source of India's energy needs, a major economic partner in trade and 
investment. Over 3.5 million Indians are engaged in the economic 
development of the Gulf countries." So, if this attack does take place, what 
would happen? The geo-political situation in the whole region will have to be 
redrafted. It will have its own repercussions and it will very much affect us. Of 
course, we have trade relations with them. We are dependent, to a large 
extent, on them for our energy requirements. Around 3.5 million Indians are 
working in the Gulf countries. If war were to break out, it will be very difficult for 
these people to remain there. I don't know whether they would be able to 
leave during war-time. For the present, this can be kept aside. But we will 
have to face the problem of rehabilitating these 3.5 million people. Will it be a 
small problem? No; it will be a very serious problem. Therefore, I want to say 
that the Government has to, categorically, declare the policy that is being 
adopted in this particular matter. I think, the Government should, categorically, 
say that we don't agree with the tactics followed by the super-powers; we don't 
agree that they have got the right to attack any country they like. No country 
should be allowed to do that. The United States is dictating terms to the United 
Nations. We should, categorically, say that we don't agree with that also. We 
should demand that some more time should be given to Iraq. Those who are 
inspecting the arms in Iraq, should be given some more time to do the testing. 
After all these tests, let the U.N. decide whether Iraq should be attacked or 
not. No individual country can take a decision over that. The Government of 
India should make this point clear. But after observing the stand taken by the 
Government, and the reluctance and hesitation on their part to categorically 
declare their policy, I am led to believe that this Government is doing so with a 
deliberate intention of wooing the United States of America.   In that 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
case, the prestige of our country will go down.   This is what I have, to say 
about that. 
Now, I come to my next point. The President has, in his speech, 
pointed out that our economy is growing at a faster pace. He has mentioned 
that problems are being solved, and that the percentage of poor people has 
come down, etc. Unfortunately, I don't agree with the views expressed by him. 
What exactly is the real situation? For example, take the case of agriculturists. 
About 65 per cent c r me people in our country depend on agriculture. The 
agricultural labour, fa rmers, etc. depend on agriculture only. For the last 3-4 
years, because of the heavy .all in production of the agricultural products, their 
life has become miserable. They have suffered severe losses. And, not only 
this, they are heavily indebted. Therefore, out of desperation, some of them 
have committed suicides.   So, this is the real situation. 
Now, I come to the question of workers. Of course, it has been 
claimed in the President's Address that the Government is committed to 
safeguard their interests. But, now, what is happening? In the public sector 
units, workers are being sent out on VRS. About eight lakh people have 
already been sent out on VRS. And, now, in all the public sector undertakings, 
the second round of sending on VRS has already started. The State Bank of 
India has decided that 60 per cent of its employees --that means more than 
1,20,000 employees -- will be sent out on VRS. If this goes on, what will be the 
situation? Of course, they will get some money at that time, but there is no 
safety. No arrangement is being made to provide them protection, in the form 
of providing alternate employment opportunities, etc. Nothing of that sort is 
being done. It will create problems. The same thing is happening in the private 
sector also. Our traditional industries, for example, beedi, weaving, cashew, 
coir and a large number of other industries are all in crises. There is no work. 
Workers are not getting proper wages. On the other hand, the Government is 
trying to amend the labour laws in a retrograde manner. Under the 
circumstances, workers are very much worried. That is why, a large number of 
Central Trade Unions like AITUC, CITU, HMS, and UTUC have joined together 
and decided at a Convention held in Delhi, on 15 th of last July to carry on a 
march to Parliament on 26 th of this month itself. But, unfortunately, the 
situation is such that it will be very difficult for us to convene ttie« march. The 
police are not allowing us.    I, alongwith Shri Gaya Singh, met hon. 
240 

[24 February. 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Home Minister. We talked to him. He was very cooperative. He talked to the 
Governor, and the Governor talked to the police officers. The police officers 
said that we would not be allowed to get out of the Ram Lila maidan. And, 
now, they are saying that we may be allowed to go a little ahead, but, 
thereafter, we will be stopped. In a democratic country like ours, why can't the 
people be allowed to carry on marches and demonstrations in streets to 
express their grievances, to raise their demands, etc? 
In the case of Iraq, in all the capitals of various countries in the world, 
big demonstrations took place. In London, it was reported that 20 lakh people 
participated in the demonstrations, but nothing happened there. They 
expressed their views against war and for peace. They raised slogans and 
conducted demonstrations. Why, in a country like ours, people are not allowed 
to conduct demonstrations and to carry on march. Therefore, I think, the 
Government should reconsider this issue. 
Thirdly, I would like to say that the President's Address, has raised 
some hopes that the Tenth Five Year Plan, which has already been approved 
by the Government, as well as, the National Development Council, is going to 
be implemented. Of course, the target set, that is, eight per cent growth is 
very high. It has been stated that about five crore jobs would be created. All 
these are laudable objectives, but, Sir, I am doubtful whether these targets 
would be achieved. Madam, for implementing the Plan, what is first required is 
resources, the financial resources. The first suggestion that is made in this 
regard is to raise 10 billion every year. That is the proposal. Madam, from 
1991 onwards since we begun to implement the globalisation or liberalisation 
programme, we have been trying to get more and more Foreign Direct 
•Investment. For the first nine years, what we have got is only $ 27 billion. 
That means, on an average, we are getting only $ 3 billion every year. During 
the last two years, I think, perhaps, it might have gone up to $ 4 billion, and, 
this year, we are getting round about $ 4 billion only. So, will it be possible, in 
the coming years, to have a sudden jump from $ 3-4 billion to $ 10 billion? 
This is one thing. 
The second thing is, another source on which we can depend on is 
the revenue resources. In the President's Address also, it has been said, "In 
the case of realisation of tax revenues, we are lagging behind." On most 
occasions, in several cases, we could not even fulfil the budgeted 
241 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
targets, and the realisation was less. Therefore, the President has stated in his 
statement that two things will have to be done in this regard. The first thing that 
he has said was that realisation of tax will have to be increased, and the other 
thing which he has pointed out was that the governance should improve. 
Madam, let me say that it is always being said that workers are the main 
hindrance in the production and the working of the industry; it has been said 
that workers are preventing the flow of the FDI into the country. But, Madam, 
what will happen to these FDIs? All of them say that they want to come 
forward and express their readiness to invest money here, and pursue it for 
three or four years, but they do not get the necessary clearance from various 
Government Departments. The things do not move forward. Therefore, most of 
the people may leave. After waiting for two or three years or even four or five 
years, they will leave. Why is it so happening? It is because of the red-tapism, 
and also because of the long-binding procedures. These are basically the 
main stumbling blocks. Why couldn't this problem solved so far? How can we 
expect that it would be solved within the next one or two years? I do not think it 
can be solved within that time. 
Madam, the third thing is with regard to the tax. Even in a country like 
India, the number of people who are having -- according to the tax figures -- an 
annual income of Rs. 10 lakhs and above is only 54,000. This is the position in 
a country which is having a population of more than one billion. Madam, about 
15-20 per cent people is expected to be in a better-off position, i.e., their 
economic position has improved. If it is so, wny has the number of tax-payers 
remained so low? Madam, what happens is, only the Government employees 
or the teachers or the employees in the private sector are taxed. They will all 
be taxed because their salaries are fixed, and, from them, the tax could be 
realised at source. Therefore, it is being realised. But most of the people who 
are able to give tax, are out of the tax net. That is one thing. The other thing is, 
even if some taxes are levied on these people, most of them evade paying tax, 
and become defaulters. That is what is happening. That also is not being 
looked into seriously. Therefore, it is the question of resources. Another 
question that is to be considered in the case of resources is that of small 
savings or the national savings. In our case, the percentage of national 
savings is coming down from 25-26 per cent to 22-23 per cent. That is what 
has nappened. The steps that have been taken by the Government to re-fix 
the interest rates and to reduce the interest  rates have already proved to be a 
sort of 
242 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
disincentive to the depositors. Therefore, the possibility of increasing the 
national savings is also becoming difficult. Moreover, there are reports that the 
Government is intending to persuade the small investors to approach the 
stock exchanges, and in that case the national savings will not be raised. 
Therefore, resources do not have any prospects also. In such a situation, 
because of the difficulty in raising resources, the targets could not be attained. 
With regard to the growth rate, the first year of the Plan is going to end by 31 * 
March. But what will be the growth rate? In the Budget, it was estimated 6.5 
per cent. Later on, it was assessed 5 per cent to 5.5 per cent. Now, it has 
been assessed that it would be 4.4 per cent. Thus, we could attain only that 
much growth rate. If you look at the previous years also, we could not attain 8 
per cent growth rate during the last ten years. In some years, we have 
reached around, above 5 per cent or, at the most, 5.5 per cent. Therefore, it 
will be difficult, or, I think, it will be impossible to attain these targets, and if 
targets are not being attained, the other expectations also will be belied. 
Therefore, my suggestion is that the Government should seriously consider as 
to how the Plan could be implemented and as to how the resources could be 
realised. 
Thirdly, I would like to say in respect of communalism. The President 
has stated that Gujarat election has strengthened the democracy. He has also 
stated that we should see that communal disturbances or riots do not take 
place in any part of the country. What is happening in our country? Of course, 
in Gujarat the BJP had won the election; they had come to power. I do admit. 
But, at the same time, everyday the leaders of the VHP are proclaiming from 
the housetops that they will repeat what was done in Gujarat. What was the 
peculiar nature of developments in Gujarat? In Gujarat, peopie were 
communally divided. In fact, the people belonging to the minority communities 
were being persecuted. But, it is a fact that people belonging to the minority 
communities in Gujarat are very much afraid of their future. They are also 
complaining that when other developments took place in Gujarat, even when 
certain relief measures were announced, certain compensations were 
announced, most of the people who deserve relief and compensation were 
not given those benefits. That complaint is also there. Now, the VHP leaders 
are saying that this countrv will have to be made a Hindu Rashtra. It is very 
difficult to believe that these things are being said by these people without the 
knowledge and consent of those who are in power, or else, nobody will dare 
to do that. Every day they are coming and saying, this country -- a secular, 
democratic 
243 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
country according to the Constitution -- will be made a Hindu Rashtra. Then, 
they again say that in Ayodhya the temple will be constructed. That problem is 
there. But they are adding to the problems. Take, for example, what is 
happening at Dhar near Indore in Madhya Pradesh. A problem was also 
created there. Then in Chikmagalur, another problem was created. Recently 
some of them have said that 3,000 mosques will have to be returned. Then 
somebody said that 30,000 mosques will have to be given. When all these 
things are being freely propagated from the housetops, the Government keeps 
mum on these matters. No POTA is applied against them; no law works 
against them. That is what is happening. Therefore, if the Government is 
serious to see that secularism is maintained, communal disturbances are not 
taken place and communal harmony is maintained, the Government will have to 
take serious steps with sincerity, or else, it won't help us. Now, I come to the 
other question. Madam, it has been stated in the President's Address that, it is 
the prime concern of the Government to safeguard the interests of the weaker 
sections and the working class, and to ensure welfare measures for them. But, 
what is happening? There are several labour laws in the country, and I can say 
this with confidence, that in larger parts of the country, none of the provisions 
of the labour laws is being implemented, and I am prepared to prove this fact. 
In several places, the Labour Department is quite ineffective, it is dormant, and 
that is the situation. The existing labour laws are not being implemented. That 
is one thing. Secondly, there was the Provident Fund Scheme. Under this 
scheme, a higher rate of interest used to be given on the amounts that were 
being accumulated, and finally, the workers used to get the benefit of it. But 
now, they are reducing the rate of interest on such accumulation in stages, in 
phases. Again, they are thinking of reducing the rate of interest. If this is the 
situation, how can they say that they are looking after the welfare of the 
workers? How are they favouring the workers? Madam, in the beginning, I 
have said that workers are being thrown out of employment on the basis of the 
VRS or they are being retrenched on one pretext or the other. In a country like 
ours, the biggest source of employment is the cottage and village industries, 
and not the modern industries. Of course, modern industries are also 
necessary. But, at the same time, compared to the modem industries, more 
employment would be provided by the traditional industries and the cottage 
industries. That is the situation. What is the condition of these industries? They 
are being neglected completely. Their problems are not being attended to, and 
whatever concessions used to be given in the past for the cottage, handloom 
and weaving sectors, they are 
244 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
being withdrawn one after another. Therefore, they are all in great difficulty. 
Therefore, that claim has also been negated. 
Regarding education, in the President's Address, it has been claimed 
tl *t in the matter of compulsory elementary education for children between the 
age of 6 to 14 years, all of them will be provided free education. But, what was 
the result? Last year, the amount allotted for that pioose was only half of what 
was required, and now, reports are regularly appearing in the Press, that this 
year also, that is, during 2003-04, the Budget allotment for this purpose is 
going to be very meagre, and this task will remain unfulfilled. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Chitharanjan, will you conclude now? 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: So far as the question of higher education 
and technical education is concerned, what is happening here? Now, the 
engineering colleges and the medical colleges are being given to self-
sustained institutions. What are they doing? If a student wants an admission in 
those institutions, in that case, in some institutions, you have to give Rs. 35 
lakhs. Leave aside the high fees that he has to pay, a capitation fee up to Rs. 
35 lakhs is being charged for these courses! Even for certain courses, which 
are not so important, Rs. 12 lakhs to Rs. 14 lakhs are being charged. Even for 
a B.Ed course, lakhs of rupees will have to be provided. Therefore, if these 
things go on, people belonging to the poorer sections, the lower middle class, 
and even the Government employees, including the higher ups, won't be able 
to get their wards admitted in the aforesaid courses in these institutions. How 
much salary does the highest Government officer get? I think, it is somewhere 
between Rs. 30,000/- and Rs. 40,000 per month. How can that officer make up 
Rs. 25 lakhs or Rs. 35 lakhs for the admission of just one of his children in the 
medical or engineering college? How can he raise that money? Here, we all

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Thank you, Madam, for giving me an 
opportunity to speak on the Motion of Thanks to the President's Address 
moved by Dr. L.M. Singhvi. Madam, exactly, an year ago, while participating in 
the similar debate, I expressed serious concern about the deteriorating 
economic situation in the country and the lack of proper debate and 
discussion on such vital issues as economics that directly affect the quality of 
life of one billion people of our country. It is very unfortunate that even after 50 
years of Independence, we still have not come to realise as to what our 
priorities are. Unfortunately, we seem to be getting overwhelmed, at regular 
intervals, by many historical aberrations for which generally there are no easy 
solutions. 
Madam, I want to emphasise that we cannot turn the clock back. We 
cannot correct every mistake that had occurred some 500 or 600 years back. 
We are now living in a more civilized world, in the sense-that there are many 
checks and balances that seek to prevent flash points. We are all witnessing 
how the countries like Germany, France are able to stand-up to the aggressive 
posturing of a unipolar country like the United States, vis-avis Iraq. The world 
has become a very small global village. Thanks to the technological 
developments that have taken place in the country, the distance across the 
globe has really shrunk. The world is very different now than what it was 
earlier during the last 5,000 years. In a sense, it will not be possible any more 
for the mightier nations to subjugate the weaker nations and occupy the weak. 
We used to call the historical leaders like Alexander and Napoleon as the 
greats. But they are no longer the greats. In true interpretation of the term, 
they can be described as land-grabbers. The true leaders who have inspired 
us and whose lives have inspired us are Mahatma Gandhi, Baba Amte and 
Mother Teresa. They deserve to be called the greats, not the land-grabbers 
like Alexander because the great people, disregarding their personal interests, 
have tried to reach out to those underprivileged who have been suffering, 
regardless of the religion and caste of the person. Every religion - although it 
came into existence by promising greater peace and prosperity, order and 
tranquillity - the world history shows, unfortunately, was the source of the 
greatest sorrow and suffering. Many battles were fought in the name of 
religion. We have heard about the Crusades which were fought for 300 years. 
They have been fought in the name of religion, sectarianism, bigotism and 
fanaticism. We are seeing today the problems between various sects of 
Christianity, Islam and Hinduism.  Still, we can authoritatively say that the 
problems have

country, a decision was taken by the Constituent Assembly to make 
secularism as edifice of this country, as the very foundation of our 
constitutional and democratic set up.

all controversial issues -- the need of the hour is to empower the people, to

issues which we, think, will assuage the feelings of the people. But, in fact,

as the Prime Minister has proclaimed that India is going to achieve 8 per cent 
growth rate -- we should achieve it. That is the imperative need of the hour. 
And, this 8 per cent growth rate has to be achieved over a period of time, say, 
10-15 years, in order to provide respectable living to the people of our 
motherland. Sir, the Central Statistical Organisation has recently announced 
that the growth rate for this year 2002-03, which is the first year of the Tenth 
Plan, will be somewhere around 4.4 per cent. It is much, much lower than what 
we have expected and proclaimed to achieve. The Ninth Five-Year Plan 
completed in the month of March, 2002 with an overall GDP growth rate of just 
above 5 per cent. That, even in the first year of the Tenth Plan, that is the 
current year, India registered a meagre growth rate of 4.4 per cent, which is 
ominous. And the reason which has been given by the President of India in his 
statement, which reflects the opinion of the Government, that because of the 
drought situation the GDP growth rate has gone down. So, for a large country 
like India, in any given year, we will have droughts, floods, earthquakes and 
different types of natural calamities and this reason alone cannot be attributed 
for the reduction in the growth rate that has been achieved. The planning 
authorities should have taken into consideration all these facts before fixing 
the target rate of 8 per cent. Otherwise, we will be only ending up by extending 
the excuses, at the end of every year, as we have done by the end of the Ninth

there is no justification for such a low growth rate, especially in the last three 
years of the Eighth Plan, we could achieve 7.2 per cent. Therefore, the

"the recent dip in the estimates of the GDP growth has been almost entirely 
due to the shortfall in agricultural production." That is why, I am emphasising 
this point. This has, once again, highlighted the need to rescue our agriculture

investments in irrigation and in all other inputs that increase the farm 
productivity. So, the Government has realised the necessity of stepping up the 
investments in agricultural and industrial infrastructure. Sir, the fact that a drop

growth makes it much more painful because 66 per cent of the work force of 
this country depend on agriculture, and naturally, their real income has fallen 
substantially. Sir, we have been continuously repeating this aspect and I feel 
they deserve to be reiterated on the floor of the House. As per the select 
macro-economic and financial indicators, provided by the RBI, the growth in 
agricultural production was 2.2 per cent for the decade 1992-2002 as against

60 per cent over a decade's time. Because this sector happens to be the key 
sector for the economy of our country which employ the largest work force. It 
has got much greater bearing on the overall economy of the country. This 
might have been one of the reasons for the paradoxical situation that we had 
in 2002, when the country had a buffer stock of 70 million tonnes of foodgrains

population was reported to have been undernourished. This is clearly 
indicative of the situation where a majority of the people are dependent on 
rural and agro-based economy, not having a purchasing power beyond the 
sustenance level, which is one of the main reasons for the lack of growth in the 
aggregate demand for goods. So, when a person gets the purchasing power to 
buy goods of his necessity, there is an increase in the aggregate demand for 
goods. The increase in the aggregate demand for goods will increase the 
industrial production of the country and, consequently, the people will have 
surplus money and savings so that they can again invest them in the industrial

the   developed   countries.     Then,   irrigation  facilities  have  to  be

Sir, I have narrated all the constraints that have been faced by the 
country, and the reluctance on the part of the Government of India to address 
the needs, the problems, on priority. Sir, at this rate, how do we achieve this 
8% growth rate in real terms, especially with the given trend -in the very first 
quarter, the growth rate that has been predicted by the Statistical Organisation 
being at 4.4%? My advice is, you better increase your spending on creation of 
capital assets. Of course, it has been said and it needs to be repeated again. 
You increase the spending on creation of capital assets, even if it means 
increase in fiscal deficit, so long as it doesn't result in additional revenue 
deficit. 
I quote one historical example. When China faced a 3.5% fall in 
prices, in the second half of 1998, and reduction in the aggregate demand for 
various products, for the first time ever it had experienced in decades, the 
Chinese Government didn't think twice on stepping up the Governmental 
expenditure in various infrastructural sectors, like irrigation, power and others. 
They speeded up the implementation of the 1.2 trillion US$ infrastructure 
development. They speeded it up. In just six months' time, the Treasury issued 
additional money worth 30 billion US$ to take up various additional projects. 
This policy yielded several immediate dividends - for example, investment in 
fixed assets rose by 22.7% in the first quarter of 1999, over the same period of 
the previous year. The sharpest rise was in agriculture, at 122%, followed by 
transport and communication at 46%, and housing by 35.5%. The GDP growth 
touched 8.3%, according to the official estimates, in the first quarter of 1999. 
The industrial production registered a growth of 10.1%. These are the facts 
that are available. It is history! They have been benefited by it. Why can't we 
adopt this?

When India opened up its economy in 1991, there were great 
expectations of the flow of foreign direct investment into the country. We 
liberalised many things. We created a hassle-free atmosphere for inviting the 
foreign direct investment. It was expected to create large industrial 
Infrastructural asse ts, which, in turn, could create employment, and revenue

year. The expectation was mainly based on certain facts like India being a true 
cJemocratic country, having a free press, having independent judiciary, having 
a very big pool of scientists, with a substantial population speaking the English

expectations. At the end of the first decade, looking back into retrospect, it is

before this august House is, the number of judges is not important but the 
quality of judges is more important and then only they can dispose of a large 
number of cases. Comparison of the American system will not solve the 
problem. We should have more number of judges to dispose of pending 
cases. 
287 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
I would like to stress one more point before this august House. In 
1992-93, about Pondicherry, it ha9 been mentioned in the Estimates 
Committee, "In order to make Legislative Assembly, the Committee desires 
that powers may be delegated to this body in a far liberal manner as that has 
been done hitherto." They also recommended that in the case of difference of 
opinion between the Lt. Governor and the Legislative Council, the views of the 
elected representatives should prevail, except in matters of national security, 
law and order and such other important areas. The Union Territories Act, in 
1944 prescribed that the will of the administrator is more important than the 
Council of Ministers, the Council of Ministers is only advisory; whatever advice 
is given to the Administrator, the Administrator can even turn it down and he 
can take an independent decision. 
As early as in 1992-93 itself, the Estimates Committee had made 
specific recommendations, saying that there should be an amendment to the 
Union Territories Act and by virtue of that amendment, the administrative 
bodies should be given more powers and that the words of the Council of 
Ministers should be taken into consideration rather than the Administrator. So 
far, no amendments have been made in the Union Territories Act. Though we 
have crossed more than 12 years, still, it is only pn paper. Though the U.T. of 
Pondicherry has taken the form of a Legislative body, though there are 
Ministers, the recommendations have not been taken into consideration. I 
request the Government to make an amendment with regard to this particular 
aspect. 
Now, a word about the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is a fine 
Prime Minister. He is having a dream of turning India into a developed country. 
In his dream, he has the Golden Quadrilateral Project, covering 6,000 Kms, 
costing Rs.54,000 crores; the National Power Grid, at a cost of Rs.80,000 
crores; Inter-linking of River Waters, at a cost of Rs.5,60,000 crores; and the 
Sky Bus Metro, costing Rs.25,000 crores. The dream is good and I am sure, it 
would come true. 
I have a submission with regard to Tamil Nadu. Tamil Nadu had 
collected one crore signatures, from different parties and from different corners 
of the State and presented a memorandum to the Prime Minister, 'urging him to 
take steps for the release of Mr. Vaiko. He was a Member of this House for a 
period of 18 years; he is a Member of the Lok Sabha for six years.  The first 
signature of the memorandum is that of our leader, 
288 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Dr. Karunanidhi, urging the Prime Minister to take immediate steps for the 
release of Mr. Vaiko from detention. In spite of that, the Government has not 
taken any steps for his release from custody. 
There is a point related to this. Section 60 of the Prevention of 
Terrorism Act deals with the things as follows: 
"60(1) The Central Government and each State Government shall, wherever 
necessary, constitute one or more Review Committees for the purposes of this 
Act. 
(2) Every such Committee shall consist of a Chairperson and such other 
members not exceeding three and possessing such qualifications as may be 
prescribed." 
My submission is, as per section 60 of the Act, the Government of 
India can, and should have, formed a committee. I don't know whether such a 
committee has been formed till today or not. If they have not formed one, they 
are bound to form it under section 60(1) of the Act. This committee is Review 
Committee for every detention. If the detention is illegal, if the detention is 
unwarranted, if the detention is vindictive, if the detention is based on political 
motive... They should review the matter and take necessary steps not only in 
the case of Vaiko but also for all the people in India who have been 
unnecessarily detained in jails. I believe, the Government of India has not 
taken any steps by virtue of section 61 of the Act and has not appointed a 
Review Committee so far. If this Review Committee is appointed, the wishes 
of one crore people of the country, who have signed this memorandum will be 
taken into consideration by the Government of India. So, I request the 
Government of India to take earnest steps to see that the persons who have 
been detained unnecessarily on political grounds or due to political vendetta 
are released from jails. With these words, I conclude.   Thank you. 
SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominated): Madam Deputy Chairman, I 
thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak. Madam, I congratulate the 
Mover of the Motion of Thanks, my distinguished and hon. friend, Dr. L.M. 
Singhvi for a fine eloquent speech which has set the level of debate. However, 
Madam, permit me to draw attention to a couple of significant points and 
comment on them. They are significant and most relevant points in these 
times to governance in our country. 
289 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
The first significant point is the complete omission in the President's 
Address about any policy of this Gove rnment with regard to violence and 
perpetrators of violent acts, whoever they be and wheresoever they are seen 
perpetrating them. 
It is true that the President's Address does state that 'we must resolve 
to ensure that communal violence is never repeated in any part of the country.' 
But that is an exhortation to the people of India. There is no signal which only 
the Executive Government at the Centre can give, that all acts of violence by 
whomsoever committed and wheresoever they take place, will be put down 
with a firm hand. 
Madam, messages are frequently conveyed by silence, and the 
silence about this in the President's Address sends the wrong message, such 
as if you have the right political connections, we will look the other way.  This is 
not good for governance in a pluralistic society like ours. 
Secondly, there is no word of solace in the President's Address for 
the victims of violence, whether communal or otherwise - this is very important 
- nor any assurance of early redress. 
The arrogance of religious hatred goes uncontrolled and unpunished 
primarily because those appointed to investigate these events are as yet 
calling no one to account. 
It appears to me that in Gujarat it is not despite the appointment by 
the State Government of a Commission of Inquiry - but because of it, that 
injustice continues to remain the looming casualty of the Godhra and post-
Godhra tragedies. 
In the very first sentence of paragraph 14 of the President's Address 
it is stated that Assembly elections in Gujarat have strengthened democracy.  
Good, they have. 
But then it goes on to say that elections have ended 'a sad chapter in 
the State's history.' Madam, the sad chapter has not ended. It will not end so 
long as no redress is given to the victims of the violence that preceded the 
elections. 
290 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
A clear declaration of Government policy that communal violence 
whether by minority communities or by the majority community will never be 
tolerated, and must never be repeated in any part of the country is, I believe, 
the need of the hour. It is only such a clear declaration that will send the right 
signals to all persons in the country. 
Let me remind the hon. Members of first sentence in paragraph 54. It 
says, "Promotion of social injustice and mainstreaming of the weaker sections 
and the minorities have been the constant endeavour of my Government." 
Mainstreaming of minorities is contrary to the Constitutional mandate. 
Minorities do not require mainstreaming. They require protection, and the 
persons who can protect them and the only authority to whom they can look 
for protection, is the Government of the day. 
I looked closely but did not find anything in the President's Address to 
suggest that the Government of the day has distanced itself from current 
constant threats to minorities whether they be Muslims or Christians, by 
certain sections of the population. It is the Government's duty to gain 
confidence of the minorities and let me hasten to add, it is equally the duty of 
the minorities to do everything in their power and to see that the majority 
community is not, in any way, ridiculed or belittled. 
The President's Address devoted a paragraph to judicial reforms and 
has mentioned that this is envisaged in the Tenth Five Year Plan. Dr. Singhvi 
said that we must give the judicial system a human face. Now, what is the use 
of judicial reforms that don't ensure justice? Where is the human face of 
justice, In a country where an individual is told that he has violated the Official 
Secrets Act by being in possession of a secret document, kept in jail for more 
than six months, and then told that the document was not secret, after all, and 
set free. Any one can commit mistakes. So can the Government. But no one, 
just no one, after the mistake was discovered, has apologised to the individual 
concern - much less to offer him any substantial compensation for what was 
admittedly a wrongful confinement. If he were a citizen of a European country, 
the European Court of Human Rights would have awarded compensation, in a 
handsome sum of hundreds of thousands of Euros. I have been in Delhi now 
for more than thirty years and if there is one trait in the Northen India that I 
have noticed is no one apologises. No one says sorry! But, I did not realise, till 
now, that even the Central Government in Delhi is afflicted with this malignant 
disease. 
291 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February. 2003] 
I welcome the paragraph in the Address that the Ayodhya dispute 
can be resolved, either through negotiations between the two communities or 
through a verdict of the judiciary, which has to be accepted by all concerned. I 
believe it is a statesman-like approach. I would, sincerely, appeal to the hon. 
leaders of the minority community to envisage a possible situation of the 
verdict of the judiciary going against them. Have they ever considered that 
possibility? What will they do then? Prudence points to the path of a 
negotiated settlement. That is the only lasting way to communal peace. There 
is no dearth of eminent religious and social leaders to bring about a solution 
and pride has no place in negotiating an honourable settlement. 
Finally, there is one more important aspect. In the spirited address of 
Dr. Singhvi, on the Motion of Thanks, he has rightly described Parliament as 
not a mere 'talking-shop' or 'debating club' but as 'the national forum of our 
conscience and consensus.'   Very eloquent words. 
I only wish that the Government of the day had lived up to this ideal. 
Parliamentary democracy is a very important, facet of our Constitution. In fact, 
it is the cornerstone of it. But, I regret to say that the reluctance of the 
Government to discuss crucial and controversial matters in the House, and 
taking decision administratively on its own is fast becoming a new feature of 
governance in this country. We, in this House, are, in fact, reduced to a 
'talking-shop' or 'debating club' - and the most expensive one at that. 
I offer, as an example, the disinvestment policy of the Government. I 
have no quarrel* with the disinvestment policy. I personally do not think that 
the Government should engage in business and Article 298 of our 
Constitution, I believe, is only enabling -- carrying on business is not one of the 
essential functions of the Government. Nor do I raise any question about the 
legality of executive action taken on the recently proposed disinvestment. 
When this question was raised in this House, during the last Session, the hon. 
Leader of the Opposition requested the hon. Minister to take the opinion of the 
Attorney General, which he has now taken and has acted on that opinion. And, 
so far as this House is concerned, I believe, the matter must rest there. Since 
we must respect the Office of the Attorney General, as we must respect all the 
Constitutional offices in this country.    But, I am concerned with the propriety 
of action taken on the 
292 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
basis of the opinion of the Attorney General. Legality is not the only facet of 
governance. Propriety is an equal, if not more important, facet. Just as 
corporate democracy requires that even when decisions can lawfully be taken 
by a company's Board of Directors, it is but proper that it should be placed 
before the shareholders of that company for their approval. So also, vital 
national policy decision on disinvestment, even if already taken, should have 
been, as a matter of propriety, placed before the Members of Parliament, 
including the Members of this House, for their approval. It could only then be 
effectively discussed and debated. And, the hon. Minister of Disinvestment is 
amply endowed with powers of persuasion. He could help persuade and 
convince us to accept his proposal. The studied reluctance of the Government 
of the day to bring controversial matters to Parliament is slowly eroding the 
principles of Parliamentary democracy. Bypassing Parliament on vital issue of 
policy is a bad precedent and does not augur well for the future. Madam, 
comparisons with China are odious simply because we do not have the same 
political system as in China. If we were in China, there would have been 
no.debate on disinvestment; there would have been no debate on Ayodhya; 
there would have been no debate on the President's Address. I may not agree 
with what this Government does or does not do. But, I think, we should all 
agree that this system of Government in our Constitution gives us the largest 
measures of freedom. With these few reservations, I have joined the Motion of 
Thanks on the President's Address. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Madam, I reiterate what my 
colleague Shri Fali S. Nariman has said. When he says that Parliament is the 
supreme body, the supreme forum of national consensus, I agree. The 
President's Address, as we know, is really a Government document. I have 
high respect, regard and affection for the President. But, as we all know, the 
President only reads the Address, which is really a document of the 
Government. This President's Address, perhaps the longest ever, looks more 
like a PIB release with all types of so-called achievements, big or small. But 
behind this, it does hide the fundamentals of the Government's policy, and this 
governance which is divisive, not merely in terms of religion. We all know that 
it is divisive in terms of religion. But in a very insidious way. It is also divisive, 
as far as the social and economic status of people are concerned. It divides 
people in terms of religion, we all know. It also divides the rich and the poor, 
the 'haves' and 'have-nots', the socially high and the socially low.    On the one 
hand, the Government is dividing the 
293 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
people of this country, destroying the national unity; on the other hand, it is 
opening wide the doors of this country and its economy, not in great shape, to 
the intents of the profit-making multinational corporations and the 
Governments behind them. This is happening in India. This is happening in 
every country of Asia, Africa and Latin America, at this point of time. What we 
object to, is that this Government is helping and welcoming the efforts at profit 
making by the trans-nationals in everything because people in Developing 
Countries do not really count, even in the spheres of human rights of people, 
fundamental human rights of people, as far as in the case of education or as 
far as health is concerned. Now, this grabbing and profit-making, which looks 
at every thing as only a business and an opportunity for trans-nationals who 
have been allowed entry here and welcomed by the Government. All this is 
being kept under wraps. Therefore, I would just point out here what I have said 
with reference to this very important basic subject which leads to the thought 
process of people, which will decide the future of this country, that is, 
Education. If you look at this book, National Curriculum Framework for School 
Education, which has been produced by the Government itself, you will find a 
clear reference to an educational system that has a dual role. That you will find 
at page 11. It says, "There must be a system of education for those with high 
IQ and emotional quotient." The IQ is a criteria, which had been started in the 
United States, and has been debunked there. The United States wanted to 
give, what we would call in India a non-formal or alternative education, to the 
blacks on the ground that they had inferior IQ. Here, in India, we have added 
'emotional quotient' to the 'intelligence quotient'. The 'emotional quotient', 
which is the creation of this Government, means that those students, who 
have a high spirituality, must be given a special and higher education. Who 
have a high spirituality? Those who don't have to work have a high spirituality. 
The working class cannot afford to have a high spirituality. They are busy 
earning their livelihood. Therefore, that is how, this new curriculum framework 
divides the social elites from the working class. Madam, Deputy Chairman, to 
further elaborate the point, I would like to refer to page 90 of this book. It says 
that whilst those with high Intelligence quotient and emotional quotient will get 
elite education, the rest would get vocational education. And, who are the 
people targeted to get vocational education? They are: the women, the 
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes and the physically-challenged 
persons. So, all these people, put together, are to be imparted vocational 
training. And those with high spiritual quotient should get elite education.   This 
is how, at the very 
294 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
beginning itself, two classes are being created for children and this is how the 
gap between the elite and the poor masses is being widened. This is how 
divisiveness is being created in the social and economic status of this country. 
We all know, how this Government depends for its survival, for its progress 
on dividing people, on religious lines. This is what is being written in the textbooks 
that follow the national curriculum. To begin with, I shall first refer to this great 
textbook in Social Sciences, named, 'Contemporary India', brought out only a 
couple a months ago, for students of class IX. In this book, there was no 
reference, whatsoever, to the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi by Godse. The 
point had been completely left out. In this textbook, the minorities of our country, 
especially, the Muslims and the Christians, have been defined as anti-nationals, 
and that they played no role in the Freedom Struggle of our country. It is even 
mentioned that the founder of the Aligarh Muslim University was a communal 
element and he was a separatist. This is mentioned in Chapter 3, page 21 
onwards of this book. 
Incidentally, I would like the officials of this Government to please look 
at the edition of this book. This book has two joint editions. One is August, 2002 
edition and the other is September, 2002 edition. On both these books it is 
mentioned, 'first edition'. How can a book have two first editions? This is 
something which I am unable to understand. There is another an August, 2002 
edition, which I am now referring to. Then, there is September, 2002 edition, 
on which it is mentioned that it is the first reprint of October. All this is very 
confusing. The officials in the department must inquire into this. They also look at 
the number of print orders given. For the first edition of September, 2002, a print 
order of 3,75,000 has been given and for the August, 2002, edition 2,25,000 
print orders were placed. That makes a total of 6,00,000 copies. For whom so 
many copies have been printed? In the previous years, never have so many 
copies been printed for Class IX Social Sciences students. It has never gone 
beyond 2.5 lakhs. Why were so many English copies published this year? The 
number of English and Hindi copies taken together would be more. But, for the 
present, let us keep the number of Hindi copies aside. Why were so many English 
copies published? The matter is questionable because the main user of this 
book, the Delhi Government, and many private schools, had refused to use 
that book. There is hanky-panky in this. There is something fishy in this.  The 
Department should look into this. 
295 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
The point which however I would like to highlight here is the way 
this textbook communalises the situation. While communalising, it also 
gives wrong facts, historically. For instance, it is mentioned that Goa, 
Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli were, collectively, called Goa. It is 
like saying, during the British Rule, India was called Delhi because the 
Government was based in Delhi. This is the type of historical and factual 
inaccuracies given in this book. Not only that... (Interruptions)... they also 
glorify things. In this book, there is a reference to communal Muslim and 
Christian organisations and their anti-national activities. But, as far as other 
communities are concerned there were no communal elements. On page 
61, it is mentioned that Dadra and Nagar Haveli was captured by the Jan 
Sangh. This is totally against history. The Chief Minister of the then 
Bombay State, went on to become the Prime Minister, Shri Morarji Desai. In 
Volume II of "The Story of my Life", written by Shri Morarji Desai, at pages 
47-49, it has been written, how he had directed the Reserve Police to 
encircle Dadra and Nagar Haveli, so that Portuguese troops did not come. 
Then, it has been written, when the Portuguese police officers which were 
four or five in number, saw the Reserve Police which looked like a military 
force, they did not attack and ran away into the adjacent forests. There 
was no fight whatsoever. No fighting took place. That is what Mr. Morarji Desai 
said. Why do you want to glorify Jan Sangh on wrong facts? I am sure that Jan 
Sangh has done some good, but not this. This is what the historians should 
really advert to. There are people who know the facts. There are people who 
were part of this process and were fully aware of it. (Time bell rings) Madam, 
please give me five minutes to make some important points. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Faleiro, a lot of time has been taken.   
We have to accommodate all the speakers. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: Madam, that is true. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: You are taking the time of your Party 
speakers. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: Madam, I just want to say that this 
Government is trying to divide the country on social, economic and religious 
basis. On the other hand, it is welcoming all the trans-national corporations 
which are trying to gobble up our educational system.   Until 2002) in fact, 
296 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
until 14 th January, 2002, the position was that, at school level, no student 
could have foreign schooling unless he was a son or daughter of a diplomat or 
a foreigner, or her or she who had intended to pursue a course which was not 
available in India. Now, after 14 th January, 2002, anybody, whosoever it may 
be, can take up here at school level itself, any course abroad. All the big talk 
of the hon. Minister about Indianisation, spiritualisation and nationalism is 
meaningless. Now, for a student, who wants to do any course from Britain, or 
France or America, nobody's permission is required to be taken. That thing 
has been waived. Therefore, again, we are going to create, in this country, two 
classes of people. One, who have their education from foreign countries, even 
at the school level here and the others who have their education - third rate 
education - at the schools, the Government is providing in the name of 
informal education. The more we abuse Pakistan, the more we are following 
their system, because this system is prevailing there. There also the elite 
people have their education in the Western model and the rest have their 
education in Madrases. Even in my own State, Government has clcsed 
Primary Schools and handed them over to Vidya Bharati. This is being done at 
a time when Pakistan and Afghanistan, which have their educational system 
on fundamentalist group basis, are trying to become more liberal. This is what 
appears to be happening. We are, tragically, following the reverse mood, that 
is, moving from secularism to communalism, while it appears from the reports, 
that in Afghanistan and Pakistan people are trying to move, to some extent, 
however limited it might be, from a fundamentalist type of education to a 
liberal education. {Time bell rings) I just want to say this and conclude ; At this 
point of time the Ministry of Human Resource Development and the Ministry of 
Commerce are busy preparing proposals for opening our education system to 
foreign business concerns. The Government should inform this House what 
they intend to do next month at GATS. It should take the consensus of this 
House, because GATS is an irreversible process. It cannot be reversed by 
future Governments. GATS process is not subject to Indian courts.   It is 
subjected to their own courts. 
AN HON. MEMBER: Are you referring to GATS or WTO? 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: I am referring to GATS. I have found 
one Vice-Chancellor who does not know what GATS is all about. This is 
because of secrecy. And you should not be surprised if we don't know what 
GATS is. GATS is a General Agreement on Trade in services which is part or 
a branch, a follow-up of WTO. The Government must discuss this 
297 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
issue in this House. It should inform the House what it intends to do next 
month in terms of commitments and opportunities available under GATT in the 
field of education and health. The Government must withdraw the book 
"National Curriculum Framework for School Education" which is divisive and 
destroys the unity of the country for now and for the generations to come.

*104. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to State: 
(a) what steps Government have taken to tap the newly discovered gas 
reserves of Andhra Pradesh coast by Reliance Industries;

(c) by when commercial use of gas reserves is likely to start?

RAM NAIK): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c)The consortium of Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL), and Niko 
Resources Limited, Canada, has reported four gas discovereis in the deep 
water offshore block, KG-DWN-98/3, off the East Coast in the Krishna 
Godavari (K.G.) Basin. Initial estimate s made by RIL, the operator, indicate 
total inplace gas reserves of about 9 trillion cubic feet. The discoveries are 
being appraised for determining commerciality for which the procedure with 
time frame has been provided in the Production Sharing Contract (PSC). 
Commercial production will depend upon establishment of 
9

commerciality of the discoveries and the subsequent development plans. 
Based on industry experience, it takes about 2-4 years from the date of 
discovery to start commercial production from offshore depending upon the 
logistics, environment, markets etc. The role of the Government has been 
specified in the PSC, under which the c ontractor also has freedom to market 
the gas in India.

JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) The Government has set up a joint 
mechanism, called the Coordination and Monitoring Committee for 
identifying and taking appropriate action in regard to vanishing companies. 
Secretary, Department of Company Affairs (DCA) and Chairman, Securities

exchange.

met. On this basis out of 7050 issues which came during 1992—98,175 
companies have been identified as 'vanishing companies'. The total monetary 
exposure involved is approximately Rs. 952 crore. Out of these 175 
companies, 82 with total issue size (amount involved) of approximately Rs. 
600 crore had responded to the letters issued by SEBI and have been 
classified as 'resurfaced vanishing companies'. SEBI and DCA are taking 
action against these companies, too. 
Money can be refunded to investors in case of liquidation of these 
companies.

640. SHRI GHULAM NABIAZAD: Will the Minister of

been depleted;

of the employees; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL 
AVIATION (SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. On making 
periodical review of the fund position, it was observed that till October 2001, 
the total contribution collected from th e employees was Rs. 101.22 crore. Out 
of this cost of the annuities purcha sed for 1852 retired/deceased employees 
was Rs. 61.84 crore and actual contribution made by 1852 retired/deceased 
employees was 21 crores. Since the bene fit extended to the retired employees 
was disproportionate compared to the contribution made by the individual 
retired employees, the Board of Trustees after reviewing the fund position of 
the Trust decided to amend the nature of the scheme from "Benefit Defined" 
to "Contribution Defined" as the benefits under a Self Contributory Scheme 
have to be necessarily commensurate with the contributions made by the 
members. The amendment seeks to correct the disproportionately high 
pension benefits offered under the original scheme and bring it on par with the 
level of contribution made by each memb er. Under the proposed amendment, 
no member will receive pension in excess of the return on his own 
contribution.The excess pension alread y enjoyed by the retired/deceased 
employees is not sought to be recovered.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) Task Force on Direct Taxes has r ecommended that there is a need for 
integration of corporate tax and person al income tax. The Task Force has 
recommended full integration of corporation and personal income tax 
whereby a tax at the corporate level is levied at the same rate as the 
64 

[25 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
maximum rate of personal income tax and all dividends and capital gains is 
exempted from tax in the hands of th e shareholders. The Tax Force, has 
accordingly, recommended a corporate tax rate of 30% for domestic 
companies, being the top marginal rate for personal income tax, and exempt 
from tax all dividends and long term capital gains from listed equity. This 
recommendation is subject to the condition that the effective corporate tax 
liability is equivalent to the statutory corporate tax rate, i.e. tax incentives and 
artificial deductions should be removed and depreciation rates should be 
brought down. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) To encourage the States to tap the full potential of their taxing powers 
and to prevent laundering of non-agricultural income, the Task Force has 
recommended that a tax rental agreem ent should be designed whereby States 
should pass a resolution under Article 252 of the Constitution authorizing the 
Central Government to impose income tax on agricultural income.The taxes 
collected by the Centre would, however,  be assigned to the States. Tax from 
agricultural income or the purposes of allocation between States will be the 
difference, between the tax on total income (including agricultural income) 
and the tax on total income net of agricultural income. Where a taxpayer 
derives agricultural income for different States, the revenues attributable to a 
State will be in the ratio of the income derived from a particular State to the 
total agricultural income. A separate tax return form should be prescribed for 
taxpayers deriving income for agriculture. 
(e) and (f) Sir, the issues raised by the Hon'ble Member relate to tax 
policy. At present, when the Budgetary exercise is in process, it will not be

RAJYA SABHA [25 February, 2003] 
 
Statement 
 
Structural Adjustment Assistance Facilities Guidelines 
Some State Governments have been keen on accepting multilateral 
institutional funding to assist in undertaking fiscal and structural reforms. The 
key focus of the reforms is to bring fiscal deficit to a sustainable level and 
elimination of revenue and primary defic its. Since, in the past, there has been 
no uniformity in the Structural Adjustment Loans (SAL) being taken up by 
the different States with multilateral institutions like the World Bank, ADB 
etc., the institutions are being advised to ensure certain common criteria as a 
pre-requisite for accessing these facilities: 
(i) Putting in place a programme to undertake Structural Adjustment 
Programme for sustainable poverty reduction, and aimed at 
generating primary and revenue surplus and limiting consolidated 
fiscal deficit to less than 3% GSDP over a medium term (3-5 
years). 
(ii) Programme for elimination of subsidies and a sustainable 
programme for power sector subsidy elimination or containment. 
(iii) Civil services reforms including reduction in administrative costs 
of governance. 
(iv) Public Sector Enterprises reforms including disinvestments. 
In view of the need to continue with sector intervention strategies, 
particularly in the context of the Millennium Development Goals, not more 
than 20-30% of the annual commitments from World Bank/ADB would be 
taken up in the form of SAL. An overall focus on poverty reduction and 
sector specific parameters (infrast ructure, educati on etc.) which are 
ingredients of MDGs should also be reflected in the action programme of the 
SAL.The SAL should not be used for meeting revenue deficits. 
The SAL would be based on a fully  developed multi-year programme 
and negotiated as one single programme with multi-trache releases linked to 
achievement of specific reform mile stones agreed upon. The mufti-year 
programme would be fully laid out in the Bank's project documents, while 
the, legal agreements for allocation of funds may be processed separately for 
different tranches. 
90 

[25 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Requests of State Governments for availing of this facility with clear 
monitorable indication for the above programme would be then discussed by 
GOI with the World Bank and the State concerned. Appraisal and negotiation 
stages would follow, depending on the States' commitm ents to the FRF 
facilities. 
Once the loan is put through and is under implementation, where the 
adjustment programme of the State has fallen behind by six months or is 
likely to be pursued further, the adjustment programme could be called off 
and the remaining undisbursed assistance cancelled.

enterprises in the rural areas of the country. The objective of the SGSY

M.H. Kania Committee on demutualisation of Stock Exchanges 
703. SHRI R. S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the M.H. Kania Committee on Corporatisation and 
demutualisation of Stock Exchanges has recommended the abolition of 
regional stock exchanges in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, alongwith other recommendations; 
(c) whether the Government have examined these recommendations; and 
(d) if so, the Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and 
(b) The Kania Committee has noted that the concept of regional stock 
exchange, which was introduced in the days of manual trading and open 
outcry system to encourage mobilization of resources and development 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [25 February, 2003] 
of equity cult across the country, has lost its relevance in the days of 
automated trading.The Group therefore felt that the concept of regional stock 
exchange needs to be abolished. 
Some of the other recommendations of the Committee are: 
* the stock exchanges which are set up as association of persons 
and those which are set up as co mpanies limited by guarantee 
be converted into companies limited by shares; 
a common model for corporatisation and demutualisation be 
adopted for all stock exchanges; and 
* Clause (i) of section 2 of Securities Contracts Regulations Act, 
1956 would need to be amended to provide that a stock exchange 
should be a company incorporated under the Companies Act. 
* The three stakeholders viz. shareholders, brokers and investing 
public through the regulatory body should be equally represented 
on the governing board of the demutualised exchange; 
there should be specific vacancies on the board for each group of 
stakeholders; 
* the shareholder's representatives should not be functioning brokers; 
* the brokers representatives would be elected by the shareholders 
from among the brokers of the exchange; 
* the representatives of the investing public would be nominated by 
SEBI from among a panel comprising of academics, professionals, 
industry representatives, public figures and investor associations, 
none of who should have any interest in any broking firm; 
* adequate disclosures about the background of the directors of the 
board should be provided to the shareholders at the annual general 
meetings and the annual reports; 
* The roles and hence the posts of the Chairman and Chief Executive 
should be segregated. The Chairm an should be a person who has 
considerable knowledge and experience of the 
106 

[25 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
functioning of the stock exchanges and the capital market; 
*       the Chairman of the Board should not be a practicing broker; 
the demutualised stock exchanges should follow the relevant 
norms of corporate governance app licable to listed companies in 
particular, the constitution of the audit Committee, standards of 
financial disclosure and accounting standards, disclosures in the 
annual reports, disclosures to shareholders and management 
systems and procedures; 
(c) and (d) The Kania Committee report  has been approved by the SEBI 
Board on 29th November, 2002 with a modification that the voting rights of 
the shares held by the members would be determined by SEBI in consultation 
with the Government of India. Recommendations of SEBI Board are under 
examination in Government for necessary legislative changes.

THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI JAGMOHAN): 
(a)The criteria are enclosed as per Statement enclosed (See below). (b) Rock-
cut shelters at Bhimbetka, District Raisen, Madhya Pradesh 
has been nominated for inclusion in the UNESCO World Heritage List for the 
year 2003. 
The Bhimbetka Site has been evaluated in November, 2002 by ICOMOS,
